speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that on May 21, 1969 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in a letter to the International Olympic Committee in support of Montreal's bid for the 1976 Summer Olympic Games, accepted on behalf of all Canadians, the responsibility of hosting the 1976 Summer Olympic Games in that city in accordance with IOC rules and regulations, supported by a further letter on November 28, 1969 from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in view of the fact that Taiwan, as the republic of China, was and continues to be a full-fledged member of the IOC in good standing under its rules and regulations, and since this government, by interfering with normal and regular international Olympic procedures in attempting to break the precedents that have existed unhampered since Adolf Hitler's interference in 1936, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That this House instruct the minister of external affairs to abide by the official letters of support of May 21, 1969 and November 28, 1969 and leave the handling of the rules and regulations, including participation, in the hands of the International Olympic Committee where they rightfully belong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

Mr. Speaker, I thought I had made it abundantly clear before, but I am glad to do so again, that we are in no way taking a step away from our plan of bilingualism in our total government services. We indeed remain committed to the view that there is a need to provide bilingual air traffic services in the province of Quebec. We have taken certain specific steps to do so in areas where that could be done. In areas where there is a more complicated situation we were prepared to produce the procedures, having faced the difficulties and complications, and introduce bilingual air traffic service there. It is well known that a good deal of opposition to that movement did exist in certain quarters. That opposition tended to focus on the question of safety.
At all times we stated our view that safety had to be taken into consideration and that indeed we would do so. All we have done now is to re-emphasize, in ways which put beyond any doubt even for the most skeptical, that that is what we will do. But I repeated before the week end, and I repeat again now, that it is our intention, given the development of procedures which we are confident we can develop, to implement air traffic services in both languages in the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. According to the International Olympic Committee rules, and I quote:
Free entry must be accorded to teams from all National Olympic Committees recognized by the International Olympic Committee.
The city of Montreal's bid document to the International Olympic Committee of May, 1970, which was accepted by the IOC, stated: "All necessary entry permits will be avail-

able to delegations from all the National Olympic Committees" recognized by the International Olympic Committee. This bid was supported by the Prime Minister of Canada, by the prime minister of Quebec and by the then secretary of state for external affairs. In view of these facts I would like to ask the minister if he could explain to this House his government's sudden, unprecedented political interference with regard to the International Olympic Committee, specifically regarding the Taiwanese Olympic team and the government's refusal to allow that team or any other team, for that matter, belonging to the IOC free entry to Canada?

(d)	uses force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada or a province;

My right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) brought this aspect to the attention of the House a number of times during the question period before debate on this bill began. Certain incidents which have taken place over the past weekend, in particular the hostage-taking situation which caused the Israelis to go right into Uganda and free a planeload of hostages, strengthen the case that an important item of discussion in this House today should be the deletion of clause 2 of the measure before us. It is my opinion that if we delete this clause from the bill we would, in effect, kill the bill. The government has made it plain that it regards the bill as an abolition bill. If we delete clause 2 we would keep on the record capital punishment for persons who commit high treason.
I could spend many hours talking about the reasons I think we should retain capital punishment. No reason could be plainer than the events of last weekend to reinforce my statement that we in this country should retain capital punishment for high treason. Although I hope this will not be the case, with the Olympics coming up shortly in this country some hostage-taking could occur, as it did in the last Olympics. Hostages were also taken in the Uganda incident last weekend. What protection would we have in this country if hostages were taken at the Montreal Olympics?
I would like to put this very serious question to those members on the other side who are abolitionists and who voted for this bill; If 25 or 30 terrorists were to appear on the scene in Canada, would we want to put them in our jails for 25 years? I would hope not. This is why I think there should be a law on the statute books to put them to death. That is what should happen to anybody who tries to disrupt life in this country in any way.
To underline my argument against life imprisonment for 25 years, there is a man in the British Columbia penitentiary right now who has been well quoted in an article that appeared in the Vancouver Province of June 12 last, Mr. Larry Corbett. He talked about what it is like to be in jail for 25 years. This is what he said:
You know, normally speaking he'd never do that but now he's only going to get one chance. Like when you drop this 25 on a guy and he gets into a position where he can escape, he's not going to get another chance for years. They're going to swallow him up in one of these "penthouses"...
Should a prisoner be successful in escaping, he becomes desperate to stay on the loose and this puts the public generally in greater danger than before, Corbett says. If he has a heavy murder term to return to, there isn't much more than can be done to him.
Inside the prisons, Corbett says, there will be a considerable build-up of tensions resulting in more jail killings and suicides.

"It takes a hell of a lot of self-discipline to walk away from a simple little thing now. But what about when you turn around and there's absolutely no hope of me getting out for 25 years. What good am I even to myself?
"Any initiative I might have is totally lost. So now rather than restraining myself I'll be more aggressive. This guy over here isn't going to restrain himself and he's going to stick it to me. So now the paranoia sets in and you figure well, okay, I've got to get him first."
Other prisoners were interviewed and they all said the same thing. With our penitentiaries filled with people who have been sentenced to 25 years in jail, they will be vicious places to be in. The guards will have a terrible time. I can think of nothing worse than having terrorists convicted of high treason sent to jail for 25 years, with no hope of parole. These are people who will have no allegiance at all to Canada, people who have tried to destroy it. They will be in jail with others who, although they are not sweet roses, are not in prison for treason. This is why I think members on all sides of the House should seriously consider changing their minds and deleting this clause from the bill.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. member for Prince Albert raised this issue in the House a number of weeks ago. An article appeared in the Toronto Star last Wednesday which I read as I was heading back to my riding. It is by Robert Nielsen and is headlined "Terrorism may yet revive the death penalty issue". I should like to quote a couple of paragraphs from this article:
John Diefenbaker is my kind of abolitionist because he would make an exception for terrorists. Here we are dealing not with unprovable deterrence but with an airtight case for the protection of society.
When captured terrorists are allowed to live, innocent people will surely die. Children in schools and buses, hapless tourists in aircraft and airports, will be pitilessly mowed down or blown up.
This has happened again and again already. Terrorists seize an airliner full of passengers or a school full of children-killing a few incidentally or to prove their sincerity-and then threaten to murder their hostages unless a gang of brothers-in-arms, previously imprisoned for a similar crime, are set free.
I should like to stress that point, Mr. Speaker. If this country holds in jail for 25 years terrorists who kill people, how long will it be before some other terrorists hijack an aircraft or take some hostages and demand that this country free some of their citizens who are held in our jails?

As one hon. member says, they will run the operation from inside jail-and that is true. We know that the drug syndicates run their operations from inside jail. That is all the more reason the House should delete this clause, to let the terrorists of the world know that they cannot come to this country and try and pull any crazy stunts during the Olympics. If I may just conclude the article by Robert Nielsen, he wrote:
If the government concerned does not yield, they carry out their threat. If it does yield, both sets of terrorists are released to kill again. The future murders are not conjectural; killing is the terrorists profession.
Don't say it can't happen here; it already has. Mrs. Pierre Laporte is a widow to prove it.
Only a fool would predict that Canada has seen the last of terrorism within its borders. And if terrorism does come back, the debate on capital punishment will revive, hotter than ever.

I shall leave that aspect for now, Mr. Speaker, but I hope that hon. members who are listening to this important debate, or are reading it in Hansard, will seriously consider deleting this clause from the bill. This would virtually kill the bill since the government has stated quite openly that this is an abolition bill. I understand there may be some agreement among the House leaders to have some of the votes on these motions later this week, and perhaps by Thursday of this week we can vote on the motions discussed to that stage. If we could delete this clause we would defeat the bill and get it out of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak in support of the defeat of this particular clause in the bill, and there are a variety of reasons for my doing so. I mentioned the question of treason when I first spoke on second reading debate. In the meantime, my reasons for desiring to see this clause eliminated from the bill have been widened by some rather irresponsible and inflammatory statements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during his contribution to the debate. Speaking on June 15 last, the Prime Minister used expressions of high semantic value concerning the noose and the horrors of hanging a person. This, of course, is a tactic that is employed by the press; and I deplore in the strongest language I can think of the tactics used on television. Whenever they talk about this subject, their symbol for debate is a noose around the maple leaf. They do this in order to drive people away from this means of carrying out the death sentence upon those who are guilty of murder of one kind or another. We are not talking about this.
My views have no connection with hanging but, rather, with the death penalty. I even avoid use of the term "capital punishment" because that has a connotation as a result of the Latin derivation having to do with the head. I am not talking about that; I am talking about the imposition of death on a person who has taken the life of someone else. In this particular instance we are talking about treason and treachery as referred to in clause 2. The Prime Minister can make certain suggestions, if he wants, in order to get people's backs up and sort of convince some of those wishy-washy members on his side of the House that they should vote in support of this bill. Thank goodness they are not all wishy-washy.
The Prime Minister can suggest that the lives of those 11 people will be on the conscience of those who defeat the bill. This is not on my conscience now. What should be on the conscience of every Canadian is the life of those who have died and those who will die if this bill is not defeated.
I hesitate to bring forward this subject, but the Prime Minister did so when talking about treason: he delivered an inflammatory address in this connection. As the hon. member who preceded me said, Her Majesty will be here within two or three weeks, and the government is suggesting we remove from the statutes the death penalty for anyone who makes an attempt on the life of Her Majesty. What would be the case in respect of a president? Is the Prime Minister going to reinstate the death penalty when a president is involved? The Prime Minister is certainly not
Capital Punishment
thinking in terms of Canada's connection with, and value for, the Crown. It is not only the Crown which is involved in the act of treason. We all know that treason is a matter affecting the institutions of our government, and anyone who mounts a revolt or tries to overthrow or take over institutions, federal or provincial, by force is guilty of treason. If that is not a crime deserving of the ultimate penalty, then I fail to know what more serious crime there is.
This is supposed to be an abolitionist bill. I have the feeling that the government and those who drafted the bill have failed to realize that the death penalty is still very much written into our laws. The schedule of the bill provides for the removal of certain clauses of the Criminal Code and of the Fugitive Offenders Act, but there are other areas where treason and treasonable acts remain on the statute books. I am not questioning this, because this is where they ought to remain as crimes for which the death penalty should be accorded after a person is convicted by a judge and jury. I refer to the National Defence Act, chapter N-4, of the Revised Statutes of Canada. This chapter does not talk only about persons in uniform, but about every person who is held guilty of committing any one of a number of offences. In general terms, it refers to every person who does, or omits to do anything, or aids such a person who commits an offence, or abets any person in the commission of an offence, or counsels or procures any person to commit an offence. Thus, any person would be guilty of an offence.
What sort of offences are involved? For example, on'the matter of security-and this is section 65 of the National Defence Act-the death penalty is provided for a number of offences. It provides that every person shall suffer death who discloses the preparations for operations of any of Her Majesty's forces. That is one treasonable act which would undermine our country. It refers to every person who discloses, in any manner whatever, any information relating to the process, procedure, publication or document of any of Her Majesty's forces or of any forces co-operating therewith, or does or omits to do anything with intent to prejudice the security of any of Her Majesty's forces or any forces co-operating therewith. This does not refer only to persons in uniform.
Bill C-84 is a complete fraud that is being put upon the people as the abolition of capital punishment in this country. It is nothing of the sort. It is a limited abolition bill, and it is high time the real intent of the bill was made clear. Section 68 of the National Defence Act provides that every person who is a spy for an enemy is guilty of an offence, and upon conviction is liable to suffer death or a lesser punishment. Section 69 provides that every person who joins in a mutiny that is accompanied by violence is guilty of an offence and liable to death or a lesser punishment; and section 70 provides that every person who joins in a mutiny that is not accompanied by violence is guilty of an offence and is liable to imprisonment for life or a lesser punishment. It then refers to the ringleaders and suggests that, upon conviction, they are liable to suffer death or a lesser punishment.
This government is deluding the Canadian people, as it has made the practice of doing for the last four or five years. It is deluding those who are sincere abolitionists

that there is to be an end to the death penalty in Canada. This is just not true. Here we have the government trying to make lighter the sentence for the crime of treason or a treasonable act in Canada, be it against Her Majesty or against our institutions. I mentioned this in my earlier intervention in this debate which happened to be on budget day, May 25. Nobody bothered to pay any attention because the budget was the all-important thing on that particular day; but it is there in the record for May 25, if anybody wants to read it.
I fail to see how this government can put forward such a notion, depriving Canadians of all their desire to uphold, with every power in their possession, the institutions they hold dear, even to the length of putting their lives on the line to defend them. There are many of us in this House- thank God-who have done that. There are some in this House, although not too many now, who have done this even twice. I am prepared to do it a third time. This measure is absolutely unacceptable to the Canadian people. It is certainly unacceptable to me. I think I speak for a great many people in my riding and a good many people across the whole of this country who just cannot understand the reasoning of this government in abolishing treason as an offence for which the death penalty ought to be given by a jury.
The acceptance of clause 2-and I hope we will have a vote on it shortly-would have a number of consequential effects which I have listed and which I think I will save for debate in respect of certain other clauses. If clause 2 should be defeated, one of the consequences would be that clause 7 of this bill would become either superfluous or debatable, and the original section of the Criminal Code being amended by clause 7, namely, section 534, would automatically be reinstateable. I have 16 examples which follow pretty much the same pattern.
If this particular clause relating to treason or treasonable acts, whether against Her Majesty-and God help us, may that not occur-or against institutions of this country, federal or provincial, by force of arms, should be defeated, a number of very interesting consequences would occur which I propose in the course of time to mention.
I think we should look at the schedule of the bill. We have to look at it in relation, unfortunately, to clause 2, because throughout this whole part of the Criminal Code there is a suggestion in the amendments that in respect of the words "high treason or" only life imprisonment would be involved. Life imprisonment, I think, is one of the most cruel and most inhumane sentences that could be imposed by any judge. The jury may find a person guilty of an act for which life imprisonment is the penalty, but I find it difficult to understand how any thinking soul could see a person condemned to life imprisonment. What has that man to lose? I will introduce some of the horrors on the other side of those introduced by the Prime Minister. I suggest that some abolitionists volunteer to act as guardians of some of these people who have been sentenced to life imprisonment.

I am in the middle of my speech and I would prefer to wait until I have concluded it. I still think there might be a few abolitionists over there who are courageous souls who stood up against the desires of their constituents and voted for abolition who might volunteer because we will have a great deal of difficulty getting people to act as prison guards or even policemen. This will be a very serious problem in our country. I do not think the abolitionists over there have even thought of this.
A man condemned for life, whether for treason or any other act, even if his sentence should be shortened, is a man who has nothing to lose. He can kill. If he wishes to get out and kill, he will do so. That is the man's life who will be on my conscience, not the life of the man who, if we defeat this bill, will hang for his crime. Those who really concern me are the survivors of the victims of these crimes and the victims who are yet to come if this bill should pass.
I sincerely hope this bill will be defeated. I am working with everything I possess to ensure its defeat. One tiny aspect of the defeat of this bill would be the removal of clause 2 which touches on treason. The Canadian people cannot accept that treason should be set up as a crime for which life imprisonment alone is the sentence which may be given by the courts, We know, from past experience, how difficult it is to keep people in prison for two years. If people sentenced to life imprisonment want to get out, they will kill in order to get out.
There seems to be a thing about escapes in this country. I do not know quite how it happens. However, there have been a number of escapes over the last three or four years. I have lost count. Those people will be on the loose in Canada simply because we have become soft in respect of the criminal and have forgotten about the victim. Surely we are men of reason. Surely we want to protect our society. The millions of law-abiding citizens are my concern. They are on my conscience. It is not the few tens who have decided to take the law into their own hands who are on my conscience.
Many of those on the other side who are abolitionists have said that there is no deterrent value in the death penalty. I disagree. I have been told by a well known lawyer, who happens to be a member on this side and who has defended criminals, that some of them might have become murderers but for the fact that they were deterred when they became involved in a felony such as a bank robbery. They admitted to this lawyer that they refused to take a gun along with them.

speechtext:
Certainly, Mr. Speaker. I hope the hon. member will explain to his constituents how he can adopt a point of view that is so contrary to the point of view they wish him to have when expressing himself on this matter.
I should like to get back to the amendment before the House to delete clause 2. I started out by saying that of all the matters in the bill, this is the one that most concerns members of the House-some of them who are not basically retentionists, who are abolitionists but who feel, at the same time, that any individual who commits high treason against one's country deserves to pay the supreme sacrifice of his life for having committed treason; and I include in that group any individual or group of individuals who would perpetrate insurrection and revolution.
Indeed, if we go back a few years and think of what happened in the province of Quebec, I think most of us would agree that the Canadian people would have been outraged if the criminals had been captured and brought

July 5, 1976
Capital Punishment
before the courts, rather than being allowed to escape from this country, and if the penalty of death had been pronounced by the courts, as it should have been. But the government commuted the sentences after they had, in fact, killed one outstanding Canadian and had come very close to killing a foreign diplomat in our country.
We witness more and more the development of terrorism in the world and while, fortunately for us and our people, most of the terrorism that has occurred has been outside our country and as a result we are onlookers of events of great traumatic significance to a great many people and nations, I find it difficult for us to try to wipe it from our minds. The sort of situation that occurred in Uganda, which could have resulted in the death of a great many people and which was brought about by people committed to open rebellion against society, could have happened in this country; and if it had, it could have resulted in these people being placed in our penal institutions.
The people who look after the operation of our penal institutions have a difficult enough time without being asked to guard international terrorists and people willing to commit high treason against their country and to stop them from killing either penitentiary employees or fellow inmates. We have not been able to maintain security in our penal institutions up to this point, and the number of kidnappings that have taken place in these institutions in recent months indicates how difficult it is for those who have accepted the responsibility of operating these institutions to carry out their duties. How much more difficult would their task be if we placed within these institutions even more dangerous people who are committed to destroying society as it now exists. We cannot expect those who operate our penal institutions properly to protect society against these people on top of the difficult task they already have.
Regardless of whether in the end we vote for abolition or retention, if there is one part which should come out of this bill, that is the part. For years, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) campaigned as a commitment to himself and to the public at large, for the abolition of capital punishment. It was very courageous of him to come into this House and vote against this bill.
This bill goes further than the United Kingdom has gone. A great many countries have eliminated capital punishment for high treason and for many other crimes, but the right hon. member came into this House and stated that he could not support a bill which would achieve the end against which he had worked throughout his lifetime. He came into this House and said he would not support this bill because the government should be convinced that that particular part of the bill should be eliminated, so that with the coming of the Olympics, with many international events taking place in this country, and with the volatile Middle East situation, the people of this nation should be protected from international terrorism or any form of insurrection taking place. Those who commit those dastardly deeds should pay with their lives.
Then we come to the last but, as far as I am concerned, the most important consideration, and that has to do with our monarch. We are saying to the people of the Common-

wealth that while we are a Commonwealth country, we are not willing to give to the Queen of Canada the same degree of protection the United Kingdom is willing to give her. We are saying to anyone who might consider assassinating her that he will not have to forfeit his life for so doing. We are, in effect, saying to the Queen that there is a lesser degree of protection available to her in Canada than in any other Commonwealth country. As I understand it, of the six countries which have abolished capital punishment for high treason, none is a member of the Commonwealth. That is far too extreme a degree of abolition for the government to ask of the people of Canada, especially when the great majority of Canadians do not wish the government to abolish the death penalty, particularly as it applies to the murder of police officers or penitentiary employees.
There are many in this country who would be willing to extend, rather than limit, the number of crimes which should be punishable by death. There are many who believe that the death penalty should not only be carried out for the protection of police officers and penitentiary guards, but that it should extend to all first-degree murders when mercy is not recommended by the jury. The government is going beyond what the people ask and is extending abolition to the point where anyone who kills the Queen will only be imprisoned for 15 years before consideration is given to that person's securing parole-not necessarily receiving it, but consideration being given- and life imprisonment will be for a period of 25 years. A person 20 years of age can kill the Queen of Canada and be walking the streets again at the age of 45. One gets a terrible feeling that there is something wrong with the legislation before us and that we should do something to eliminate it.
I support the amendment of the hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) because it is realistic. It is the very least that those who believe in retention should expect from this government. I say to the abolitionists in this House that if this government is determined to place legislation on the statute books of this country which eliminates the protection which is now available to the monarch and to the Canadian public against terrorists, it should be defeated. The abolitionists in this House should be concerned because the government does not feel that the monarch or the public should be protected against terrorists, international gangsters, the mafia and people of that ilk. Those people know, when they consider committing crimes against individuals, that the worst penalty then can expect is 25 years in prison.
There must be something wrong with a government which believes that, regardless of what the people think, it knows better. That is an indication of a sickness in democracy which we can cure only by defeating the legislation of a government which takes this approach to politics. The best way to restore some respect for parliament and for the democratic institutions which all of us are supposed to love is to see that legislation which is contrary to the beliefs of the great majority of Canadians is defeated.
Surely, abolition carries with it some responsibility- and there is no responsibility on the part of a government which says to the Queen of Canada that we cannot afford to her the same protection which the parliament of the
July 5, 1976

United Kingdom is willing to provide. That parliament has existed longer than any other democratic institution in the world.
It is not responsible or realistic for a Commonwealth country to say to its fellow members of the Commonwealth that it cannot give to the Queen the same degree of protection she will receive when she visits other Commonwealth countries. We cannot provide her with that protection because the government has decided that any individual who attempts to assassinate, or who assassinates her, will only go into one of our institutions, and while there he will probably carry out the same type of crime against other persons, whether they be officers in the institution or inmates.
When an individual commits any kind of crime against the state, he should be prepared to sacrifice his life- nothing more, and nothing less.

I say to you, sir, that I will support the amendment. I hope the abolitionists in this House will support it, as an indication that we have special feeling for the Queen and our country and that we will give the ultimate protection to our Queen and extract the supreme sacrifice from anyone who does damage to our nation or endeavours to assassinate the Queen.

Mr. Speaker, it is time this government shed the "Alice in Wonderland" mentality regarding the objects and objectives of some people in society at whom this legislation is directed. It seems to me a contradiction in terms to talk about peace and security legislation and at the same time to eliminate the consequences for treasonous activity. Therefore, I plan to support this amendment which would make treason punishable by death.
The government is charged with providing good order and security for our country and its people, as well as for those people, especially heads of state, who visit our country. This good order is based on the concept of civilization. But treason denies the right of any government even to try to maintain order. This bill becomes a vote of confidence for anarchy.
In the last generation there was a notion, that has become popular in society, based upon the worship of the non-hero. There was a time when the hero was an individual who acted courageously on behalf of his country and was commended by the citizens of the country and the

government. As a matter of fact, one of our distinguished medals, the Victoria Cross, is a commendation for an act of valour on behalf of the country. But that kind of philosophy is under attack. Today we are faced with a popularization of the views of men like Marcuse who have made the non-hero popular. A man who either deserts his country or acts against his country is becoming the hero because that is seen as an act of courage. The man who goes over the hill is the hero.

We have had a very notable example of this kind of philosophy in the last few days, with the taking of over 200 hostages in an airplane and flying them to Uganda. That philosophy is still very popular in many countries. It is fine if those countries want to maintain that kind of government for themselves. Let them have it. But allied with that philosophy is the need to export the revolution. It is not good enough to have that kind of government within Russia, China, Viet Nam, Cuba or Cambodia: in order for that philosophy to thrive, the people who believe in it must carry it to other countries. There are a good many people in our country who think that our democratic institutions ought to be destroyed and are doing what they can to attack them.
Several months ago in this House, when we were dealing with the bill regarding citizenship, I spoke of the special parliamentary committee which had travelled the country to study immigration. We were confronted by these people in all the major cities and some of them were supported, would you believe, by the Department of the Secretary of State.
