speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment is one in our enlightened self-interest. If we cherish those institutions within our country which preserve democracy, which in fact provide freedom for dissenters to say what they say and what they could not do in the countries they espouse, which give us the kind of freedom that we enjoy, we cannot pass the legislation as it stands before us today. It is in our enlightened self-interest to pass the amendment before us, namely, that treasonable activity is punishable by death. Therefore, I plan to support this amendment and I shall vote in its favour.
I challenge the people who support the bill in general, who have not given sufficient thought to the implications of the bill in the case of treasonable activity, to rethink their position on this matter and to give some consideration to voting in favour of this amendment.
I began by saying that we have presented in this legislation an "Alice in Wonderland" mentality. I want to underscore that fact. The whole purport, underlying philosophy and groundwork of this bill rests upon the belief that man is indescribably perfectable, that in his most destructive state he has become that because society has treated him wrongly: either he has been deprived in his youth economically, or he has had a wrong upbringing. Somehow, all along the way we want to absolve man of the responsibility for his behaviour.
Mr. Skinner has done a lot to popularize the notion that we are no longer responsible; that we have been so conditioned by the forces of our society that we cannot make an independent decision any more. I reject that philosophy. I maintain that there are men and women in this and other countries who are deliberately villainous. They are determined and have chosen a path to do wrong. It is within the heart of every one of us to do that. None of us is immune from criminal activity; none of us is immune from inhuman behaviour. We are all victims of a depraved nature. Therefore, I cannot hold truck for that philosophy which says all we need to do is change the circumstances for criminals, give them a better environment and a little tender loving care and they will automatically become different people; give them plush carpets, nice lounges, better day-rooms and recreational areas, and they will be fine people. There are people who are determined to do wrong; people who have come to that place where they will

entertain violent notions and violent activity against the Crown, the Queen, and are determined to do wrong.
I say, again, that it is in our enlightened self-interest to entertain this amendment which will preserve freedom in our country to live in peace and tranquility. I urge hon. members to again think about their position on abolition of the death penalty and to give consideration to this amendment which will preserve the death penalty for those who are guilty of treasonable activity.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in clause 2 of Bill C-84 the Solicitor General of Canada is proposing abolition of capital punishment for any act of treason against Her Majesty, against Canada or against a province. He is also proposing abolition of capital punishment for overthrowing or threatening to overthrow the regime or for collusion with the enemy when as a country we are in a state of war. In short, Mr. Speaker, this means that the philosophy underlying the propositions of the Solicitor General of Canada, the Solicitor of the day-we hope he will not so remain for a long time-this means that any act likely to endanger the country or part of it would not be punishable by death but rather by what the minister calls life imprisonment.
As for life imprisonment, Mr. Speaker, and this is the first point I want to make, I do not believe in it since I do not have faith in the goodwill of the Solicitor General when it comes to implementing the law. Mr. Speaker, how many instances could we cite to prove that parole was granted even though we had been assured there would not be such release on parole?
We must not lose sight, in this debate, of the context in which the Solicitor General has placed us. He started with the notion that any irreversible penalty such as the death penalty is bad in that sense that it would denote that our society is prone to violence. He is himself a great pacifist who believes in the good will of all humans, that is why he tells us: "We shall apply such punishment which is not final, such as jail terms." And to make sure that imprisonment is not abusive towards the criminal the minister applies this principle which is radically opposed to the punishment provided by the Criminal Code, namely release on parole. Thus clause 2 of the bill which is before us and which amends the Criminal Code as far as murders and other major offences are concerned, mentions treason to which I referred earlier.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) suggests then the abolition of capital punishment in cases of treason. He thinks it is a serious crime to attack Her Majesty the Queen, the government of Canada, a province or the system. It is a serious crime to conspire with the enemy in wartime but it is not serious to the extent that the criminal convicted of treason should be sentenced to death as provide by the Criminal Code.
However, Mr. Speaker, if tomorrow our country were at war with any of the countries in the world, that same government would ask Canadians and the young people to fight in the armed forces to kill people they do not know, risking their lives to ensure the security and the defence of
July 5, 1976

Canada. That same minister would travel from coast to coast to ask the mothers of young Canadians to sacrifice their sons, as we can see it in the Memorial Chapel here in Parliament and where this government is proud to turn the pages to show the names of those great Canadians who fought for Canada in foreign countries where they lost their lives. Why? For the security of Canada, for the well being of Canada, to protect our ideology, our identity and our security. Thousands of Canadians risked their lives on those battlefields.
Mr. Speaker, all this is done for the security of the public. What is treason according to the Criminal Code? Treason is a threat made by one individual or group of individuals attempting to overthrow a government by force, through criminal means, threatening not only the stability of the state, but also the health and lives of citizens. This is an act of treason in general. An act of treason is also conspiration with the enemy in wartime, an act of treason is what we saw, for instance during the October crisis in Quebec, it is an act that endangers the lives of citizens and the political system as in Canada we are supposed to live in a democracy and that the most logical way to overthrow a government is democracy.
Mr. Speaker, this is the logic of the Solicitor General. We shall remember the epic fight of our ancestors against conscription, when they were told that they had to enroll to protect the country. And now, today, the Solicitor General claims that if any foreigner or any Canadian does the same thing, the death penalty will not apply.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder which side the Solicitor General is on and which aim he is trying to reach. I am trying to understand how he thinks and, Mr. Speaker, I cannot. I cannot understand why the minister supports clause 2 when Criminal Code sections 46 and 47 clearly state that everyone commits treason who, in Canada, attempts to kill Her Majesty, levies war against Canada or does any act preparatory thereto.
Mr. Speaker, if anyone did and act preparatory to levy war against Canada, the death penalty would not be applied. It means that anybody can come to Canada to levy war, and if he can be caught before destroying us, the death penalty will not be applied in his case even if he might have killed 25, 30, 50, 100 or 200 Canadians during his military operations. The minister proposes that the death penalty should not be applied for clause 2; he proposes, if somebody assists an enemy at war with Canada or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities, that the death penalty should not be applied. The minister proposes that we be docile, that we be kind, that we respect all that and that we lay the red carpet for anybody who might use force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada or a province.
The minister proposes that in that particular case the death penalty will not apply in spite of conclusive and cogent evidence. Mr. Speaker, I was in the House with several of my colleagues at the time of what has been called the October crisis. I still remember this Prime Minister snivelling on television and asking everyone to show restraint in that very grave moment; I remember the tearful former Quebec Minister of Justice announcing the death of his colleague minister; I remember the trucks of
Capital Punishment
the Canadian Armed Forces rolling down our streets, getting everyone edgy, controlling and watching all public buildings, members of parliament and ministers; everybody was on general alert, it was a very grave moment, Canada's security was at stake, particularly that of Quebec, that insubordinate province. Canada's security was so in danger that this government introduced a war emergency measures to stop that little outburst of revolt limited to one place in Quebec.
The army was even sent in small communities to watch alleged accused who could have been in collusion with people of the FLQ. We were in a state of general alert, and I remember that our party was holding a convention at Thetford-Mines at that time, a provincial convention for the federal party, and during the last night with beat of drum we were told about the death of minister Pierre Laporte. People were getting nervous and it was very grave. The army was on the look-out and everyone was calling for action.
What happened since then? The October crisis still remains to be explained. A lot of things are still unexplained in that file both to the public and members. A lot of things not only remain to be explained but once again I wonder how it was possible to bring in the army if today the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) suggests that this type of action is not serious. If that kind of situation is not serious, let us immediately abolish-and it is urgent-that emergency measures act. Let us put order not only in the Criminal Code but, to be consistent, in any other legislation.
Some will say, such events could still reoccur. Let us be logical. We are now having in Quebec the Olympic Games which are going to cost a lot of tax money paid by Canadian taxpayers. What is the cost of the military operations to ensure the security of athletes, visitors and prominent people? What will be the amounts paid and the role played by the federal government? Will it be to the extent of forbidding any traffic? This is quite a situation! I have been told that the federal contribution to ensure security will be about $100 million. But let us suppose a moment that such an act of treason does occur, in accordance with sections 46 and 47 of the Criminal Code, which the Solicitor General would like to abolish. On one hand, the federal government is investing $100 million for the security of athletes, very important people and visitors as well as for the general security at the Olympic Games to protect the reputation of the country. It is nice to see soldiers parading!
Let us suppose, Mr. Speaker, that an attempt is made against Her Majesty who will open the games, or against the officials of other countries or one of our public men. What will happen? A general alert, and after giving a good show to demonstrate that Canadians are safe, the criminals will be caught. Then they will be told: "We are sorry, we have to release you because Canada is an understanding country. You are released." The minister will put these people in prison. He will call a press conference. I can see him with his glasses, smiling and telling us that he has made some order in this area. What we shall learn is that a few years later, these same criminals or alleged criminals will be free once again.

July 5, 1976
Capital Punishment
With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to questions in the order paper which were asked recently in June about the number of convicts who are now free in Canada and who have not been recaptured yet, and this for each penitentiary in Canada. You can find this in Hansard. Mr. Speaker, how can we believe that the minister will ensure safety in Canada if he is content with putting convicts comfortably in prison and giving them a parole or temporary freedom, since the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) believes in rehabilitation.
Mr. Speaker, I am among those who believe that our society must be protected. I am among those who believe that our society, an organized society, must have the means to protect itself against external or internal enemies. Consequently, to protect ourselves, if someone wants to cause trouble of some kind in Canada, act in collusion with the enemy, make threats of revolt or of takeover of a provincial system or of the Canadian government, we must show the whole world that we have laws, we respect our citizens and we want to protect them.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I shall support the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). This is why I shall oppose the minister who is asking us to pass clause 2 according to which any act of treason against the Crown in general would not be subject to capital punishment. In my opinion, not only is the philosophy which the Solicitor General wants us to adopt dangerous, but it also constitutes an invitation to throw over our government system, no longer democratically, but by force. Mr. Speaker, God knows that more and more Canadians think that this is the only solution.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a motion to delete clause 2 of this bill which is an act to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences. We are considering one particular aspect of violent crime, and that is treason. I rise at this time simply to voice my support for this amendment.
I do not propose to go into the arguments that have already been placed on the record. Suffice it to say that I agree with what has been said and the reasons given in support of this motion. It is difficult to comprehend the government's determination at this time to pass this legislation, Bill C-84. At a time when the government has announced that it is launching an attack on violent crime, we have before us a bill, the provisions of which, I suggest, constitute an invitation to commit violent crime in this country.
If everything in this country was what we wished it to be, if there was a greater awareness on the part of people of their responsibility to their fellow man, a greater appreciation of the sanctity of life and a recognition of the rights of others, then I think we could understand why the government has taken the position it has. But when we see a growing disregard for human life, with little respect for the rights of others, for the government to bring in a measure of this kind is completely beyond reason.
I have just returned from my constituency, Mr. Speaker, and if the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) would like to

get the feel of the country, I suggest he goes to Fraser Valley East where just the other day a little girl's body was found tied to a tree. This was one of a number of serious crimes committed just recently, and as I mingled with the people and talked to them this was foremost in their thinking.
Reference has also been made to the events of this past week in connection with hostage-taking. Terrorism is flourishing today, and even in this country the very foundations of our civilized society are being threatened. Yet we are being urged to pass legislation which I believe is simply an invitation to certain people to commit crimes in this country.
People are being forced to the conclusion that they cannot expect justice from this government. I am not questioning the sincerity of the Solicitor General, but I just do not know what kind of dream world he is living in. Although it appears to be futile to try to achieve any change in this legislation, I feel I have to stand today and challenge the Solicitor General to take another look at reality in this country. People are looking for some evidence that crime does not pay. Under the present administration of justice in this country, it looks as though crime does pay. Although I am not questioning, as I say, the sincerity of the Solicitor General, I am questioning his judgment in a very fundamental fashion.
The motion before us seeks to reduce the punishment for treason. As has already been pointed out, Her Majesty the Queen of Canada is once more coming to this country, yet we are removing this safeguard for her protection. Surely to goodness, if we are to be faced with a provision like this, it could have been brought in a little later in the session instead of just prior to Her Majesty's visit to Canada. I just cannot see any logic behind this legislation. I cannot understand why we are being called upon to support legislation removing this safeguard.
That is all I am going to say, Mr. Speaker; I said I did not intend to make a long speech. I just want to ask whether there is some logic for our being presented with legislation which removes the penalty of capital punishment for the most serious crimes that can be committed and which some people are committing. I support the motion before the House.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very brief. At the outset let me say that I will lend my full support to this motion, which basically reinstates the penalty of capital punishment for the crime of treason. Treason is a most heinous crime. It is a crime much worse than murder because it is an out-and-out attempt not only to kill the head of state but to destroy the governmental system under which we live. It is, also, an act of supplying evidence or information to an enemy, allowing that enemy to destroy our country. It is a crime that strikes at the very heart of our country.
I understand the concern of the abolitionists when it comes to the crime of murder, but I cannot understand how an abolitionist could not support capital punishment in respect of a crime of the nature which would destroy our country. Murder is carried out by an individual who has no
July 5, 1976

respect for the life of another individual. Treason is carried out by a person who has no respect for his country. Does such an individual deserve to live? Should he not suffer death or capital punishment for such a crime? I, personally, believe he should and I believe the majority of Canadians feel the same way.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: And one weekend at home will tell you that.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: If you talk with those Canadians who spent some time in the armed forces during the last war and were prepared to give their lives for their country, you will know there is no question about where they stand. Yet this government says it really cannot execute those people who commit treason, because to execute is a cruel and inhumane type of punishment. The government suggests we should send them to jail for a short period of time and rehabilate them. You cannot rehabilitate the type of person who would kill Her Majesty, destroy this country or supply secret information to another country. Such people are beyond rehabilitation.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: How do you know that?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Because they don't want to be.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: And how do you know that?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) has the floor.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has some comments to make, I am sure the floor will be available to him as soon as I have completed my remarks. I would be interested to listen to any remarks he might have to make.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: We would like to have them on record.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Yes, I should like to see them on record. The people of Canada are concerned about law and order. They want a country in which they can live in peace and security. They want a country in which there is discipline. They want a country of which they can be proud, and they want a country in which they know we will have stable government, rather than a country that gives a licence to radical individuals to kill the head of state or overthrow the government, for which they receive a light slap on the wrist.
Let me spy, in conclusion, that I shall be very disappointed if all hon. members in this House do not unanimously support this motion.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: What does "Regina" mean, Les?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: My city is named after Victoria-"Regina." Kings and queens come and go, and kings and queens and-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: And so do MPs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
-members of parliament and people in public office know that they run a risk. They live with a
Capital Punishment
hazard, whether it be from a drunk in a beer parlour or a mental case who is out to kill. These people live with that hazard every day of their lives when they are in this occupation, whether you are a king, a queen, the prime minister, the solicitor general, a member of parliament, or the mayor of a city. When you accept public responsibility you are faced with the hazard and risk of the sick mind. It may be in the person of your next-door neighbour or your brother.
The hon. member who has moved this amendment asks each of us to become paranoid, like the amendment. He asks each of us to look under his bed each night. He asks each of us to suspect anyone and everyone who comes in contact with Her Majesty or anyone else in public office. I look at this amendment as a resolution to place the crime of treason in such a category that it will apply to every person, making everyone suspect.
I would ask the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) how he, as a Conservative, in his ideology, would have fared in a country that considered treason the espousal of right-wing philosophy. We have just celebrated with and complimented the United States on its two-hundredth anniversary of a revolution. Many people died fighting on both sides of that question. The king of England at the time said that was treason. I should like to ask the mover of this amendment, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw, whether they still consider the United States of America and every citizen in that country as traitors. I am sure there were a number of people in the United States in 1776, and four or five years before that, who would have been happy with the opportunity to assassinate George III. Indeed, some of them tried to seize the opportunity. George III had a fair number of what were called Tories and Whigs in jail in those days, some of whom we have never heard from since. They were there for the crime of treason because they wanted to speak out and were condemned for having to resort to violence.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Are you defending treason?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I am not defending treason, I am trying to suggest to hon. members who support this kind of amendment that they are asking all of society to join them in their paranoia. Society, the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand), and members of this House will do everything they can to protect both the person and the institution of Her Majesty and her loyal subjects.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Including putting up your life?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
The hon. member asks me something about my life. Life lasts for so long, but for the life of me I fail to understand how responsible members of parliament representing Canadians in every part of our country could ask us to resort to this mindless hysteria that reaches back into the Middle Ages. I do not understand what motivates them.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson) said he does not question the motives of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). Wasn't that big of him? He repeated that three or four times. I am not a friend of the Liberal party. Even my friends to the right will acknowledge that.

July 5, 1976
Capital Punishment
I have been a bitter enemy of that philosophy and that degenerate political party for as long as I can remember.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Order, please. I would suggest that the hon. member return to the subject.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: When hon. members are opposed to an amendment regarding treason and capital punishment, and then someone says that he does not question the motives of the Solicitor General and I take that as a direct reflection on all other members of this House. That, it seems to me, is beneath the intelligence and the integrity of the mover of the amendment and those who have spoken in favour of it. I remember, when I was a kid, that people were said to be guilty of treason.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: If he can remember when he was a kid, he has a pretty good memory.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), who was only in diapers then, should ask the people who know. The hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) know better. It was said in those days that people who were found guilty of treason should be shot. There were pamphlets and newspaper advertisements to this effect. Some hon. friends to my right might agree with those headlines and scurrilous pamphlets to the effect that the death penalty should apply to treason in the case of fellows like M. J. Coldwell and W. S. Woodsworth who were called treasonous. There was a member of Parliament who was found guilty of treason. He was convicted, sentenced and later departed. If he is still alive, he would be living his declining days in Poland. I refer to one Fred Rose. He was not executed.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would take the trouble to read Hansard for the years 1945, 1946 and 1947, he would find the reason. There were even some members of his own party who did not advocate that kind of penalty.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I am advocating it now.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
That is one instance. The hon. member might like to cloud the issue. There were people in the progressive party and in the co-operative movement, as well as the farmers and the livestock growers who took the CPR to court, who were called treasonous. Where do my hon. friends wish to draw the line concerning what is and what is not treason? The first socialist member who was elected in 1896 was accused of being guilty of treason. It was said that rather than being seated in the legislature, he should be hanged.
Mr. Speaker, for some reason or other some of my hon. friends seem to conclude that if one fails to support an amendment which calls for the death penalty for treason, somehow everybody else is, by definition, treasonous. The hon. member for Moose Jaw was as subtle as a baseball bat with a nail in it. The hon. member for Fraser Valley East was just about as subtle. These are the kinds of laws that people such as Idi Amin, Joe Stalin, Adolph Hitler and

Mussolini like. They like those kinds of laws about treason. They not only like them, but they implement them.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: They did not even bother charging the people; they just shot them.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: You bet they did. Adolph Hitler, Mussolini and Joe Stalin did not bother with the formality of trying someone for treason: the right to dissent went down the drain. Let us assume the worst. Let us assume that some megalomaniac, some nut, assassinated the Queen, the king, the prime minister, the leader of the opposition, or the Solicitor General. That is a hazard which confronts everyone in public life. There have been many incidents. There was a case of an irate taxpayer trying to kill the local mayor. I guess that would be called some kind of treason.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, neither the Queen nor the Crown have asked for this. The royal prerogative has not asked the death penalty if there should be a crime involving the killing of a royal person. This has not been asked for, yet the royal succession and parliamentary democracy continue. This type of thing can happen to any of us. I will make one exception. I would except that in time of war, if our country were attacked and had declared war, if one of the articles of war included execution for treason during a state of war I would, however reluctantly, accept that our society as a whole had been attacked, including the Liberals, the Tories, the Socialists and everyone else; in fact even those of us whom the public thinks of as no-good Micks. If it involved all of us, then there might be some legitimate argument for the crime of treason being a specific offence, rather than a peacetime thing as a general rule.
I should like the members who support this kind of amendment to provide some additional reason for it. The hon. member for Moose Jaw says that the Canadian people question the old adage that crime does not pay.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I did not say that.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Then the hon. member for Fraser Valley East said it. You are all the same breed of cat. If there is any one thing in which people historically believe, it is that crime has paid, and has paid very well, thank you. Hon. members wonder why the slob who grew up in a slum knocks off a couple of service stations, serves a couple of jail terms and finally ends up shooting a policeman or prison guard. Naturally, the hue and cry is that he be hanged. I do not hear anyone say that the mine owners or the contractors-who are just as guilty, in my book- should be hanged. You want people to have respect for the law. Our law is for the rich.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Hon. friends to my right would find it interesting, if they took the trouble, to learn who has been hanged in this country and who has not been hanged. Invariably, those who had the resources-particularly financial, social, business, and so forth-could resort to appeals and could go through all the procedures of our
July 5, 1976

legal process. Do not tell me that the poor, convicted murderer gets the same deal as the rich convicted murderer. He does not get the same deal. If hon. friends to my right, and those who agree with them, could show me how our law could be changed so that the poor, convicted murderer, whether it be for treason or for any other reason, could be treated in the same way as the rich, convicted murderer whose appeal is automatically launched by an appointee of the court, I would be satisfied. The poor man has no choice, but the rich man can get the top brains, the top lawyers and the best research.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
If my fine friend wants to live on cloud nine, he is welcome to it. If he did a little research into who has been convicted of murder and who has, or who has not, been hanged he will find that the law is for the rich- particularly the implementation of the criminal law.
As a member of parliament I do not want to be party to what I consider to be bad enforcement of the law by the Solicitor General and by the government-the unequal enforcement of the law. There is no equality of opportunity before our law, both in fact and in practice. I wonder if hon. friends to my right would also explain to me, when they are discussing an amendment which has to do with treason, their definition of "treason." Is their definition narrowed down to the assassination of the monarch? If so, I wish they would say so. I still would not support the amendment. In fact, the monarch, especially the one we have now, would be the last one to ask for or to expect that kind of law. Since the British have not done it for years, I find it passing strange that all of a sudden, from under a bunch of rocks or out of the woodwork, comes an amendment to the law that has not even been suggested in the British House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: It is their law now. Why are you voting with the government?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: In that case, I am learning about all these people who will use any type of subterfuge, excuse or reason, however weak.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I will continue for one minute only, Mr. Speaker. They will justify or use any subterfuge, reason or excuse to go back to what they really want, which is the death penalty. If they cannot have it holus-bolus, they will look for some other way in which they can satisfy their own feelings and the feelings of a large portion of the public.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Yes, 80 per cent of the public.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member has that kind of constituency. My mail runs the other way.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
Capital Punishment

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I want to tell my hon. friend that my mail did not run 80 per cent as against 20 per cent; it ran 55 per cent as against 45 per cent. If he would like to come up, go through all my files and read all my letters from my constituents-in fact, I put it all down in a newsletter-he is welcome. I am not relying on numbers, and I am not relying on the 80 per cent. If there were 80 per cent in my constituency in favour of abolition, I would feel that way before they ever said it, and I do not rely on numbers. But I would like to remind my hon. friend that if he or any of his colleagues want to talk to me about numbers, they do not really mean anything when you get right down to the crunch.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: They help in elections.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
If he wants to be some kind of a blob, if he wants to run with the wind, I would like to hear if the so-called overwhelming majority of his constituents felt the same way four years running. If he wants to be like a stallion sniffing the wind when he enters the gate to the pasture, that is the way he would run. If he wants to be some kind of a blob of a member of parliament, so that whatever his constituents think or whatever his newspapers say, or whatever a dozen or ten dozen letters tell him the majority of his constituents think, then frankly we do not need such members of parliament. People can always put their social security number into a computer. They would not need a member of parliament.
If the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) wants to talk about what is good for the next election, or good in terms of politics-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I did not say that.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has the floor.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your intervention, but I am sure the hon. member and I were trying to be helpful to one another.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The hon. member is making a speech. I suggest he get back to the facts.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Thank you. I seldom rise to speak in the House, and I do not speak very much.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I am a kind of a half-decent fellow, but I was invited to put my views on the record and that is exactly what I am doing. I would like a definition of "treason" from hon. members who support the amendment. What constitutes treason? I am sure the late supporters and sympathizers of Louis Riel are having second thoughts about treason. In fact, it would not be difficult to get a unanimous vote of the House to pardon Louis Riel. It is a little late, but better late than never!
I put on the record what I feel about these matters. I could be wrong, but unless the argument is put forward by hon. friends to my right in a more lucid, logical and reasoned way, I am afraid I will have to be stubborn-and I am not usually stubborn. I will have to stick to my

July 5, 1976
Adjournment Motion
conviction, to the principle, to the matter of conscience on what I think is civilized behaviour and intelligence.
The one exception I would make is in the case of a declaration of war when the nation as a whole is united to defend itself. That is the only exception I would make; and even in that situation, not only in Canada but in countless countries, most of the people who were found guilty of treason were not executed. If my hon. friend would care to check the Archives and the Department of National Defence, in the Boer War, the First World War, the Second World War, and even the Korean War there were some cases of treason-and I would like somebody to tell me about anybody, particularly in the last 30, 40 or 50 years, who was executed when found guilty. Even when they admitted guilt, they were not executed. Even the rednecked dinosaurs of those days did not advocate it, and if they did they got short shrift.
I hope the lengthy statements which have been made by hon. members in support of these amendments will not be repeated. I want to say to the hon. member for Fraser Valley East that the kind of statements he makes do nothing more than incite and encourage those nuts who can be encouraged to consider committing treason or murder.
I hope the amendment will be defeated. I hope the bill goes through as is. There may be some minor amendments, but surely there must be something more than we have seen so far. I hope we get something more. If we do not, I invite hon. friends to my right, some across the way and those to my left, to decide that their arguments have all been made. Then we can vote on all the amendments and third reading of the bill in the next couple of days.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Order, please. It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows; the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn)-Conflict of Interest- Allegation Mr. Bissonnette is linked with commercial activities of chairman of Anti-Dumping Tribunal; the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale)-Post Office- Application to Olympic stamps of provision to withdraw 12 months after issue; the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie)-Air Transport-Threatened strike of aircraft safety inspectors-Government action to ensure adherence to safety regulations.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we just finished listening to philosophy, ridicule and a bunch of nonsense from the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin).

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
In all my 18 years in the House of Commons, I have never listened to so much nonsense as I just have. The hon. member rarely makes a speech when he does not go overtime. He rarely makes a good speech unless he is heckled, and I do not blame the hecklers in this particular case. He made a very poor speech and was only heckled a little. He should have been heckled a lot more.
The amendment before the House suggests the deletion of clause 2 of the bill which refers to the penalty for those who commit treason. The hon. member did not know what treason was. As far as the bill is concerned, treason is committed by anyone who kills or attempts to kill Her Majesty or does her any bodily harm tending to death or destruction, who levies war against Canada or does any act preparatory thereto, or who assists an enemy at war with Canada. Those are the three broad definitions of treason. The clause goes on to say that everyone commits treason who, in Canada, uses force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada. One could go on and read the whole clause, but I suggest that I have read enough to provoke thought, and I hope enough for the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre to read the remaining portions of clause 2(2).
Let us consider for a moment the part of the clause which states, "uses force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada". This bill is part of the peace and security legislation program of the government. In October of 1972, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-the great abolitionist, he would like us to believe-this cabinet minister and this government brought in the War Measures Act saying that there was an armed insurrection against Canada and against the government and that there was an attempt to overthrow the government.
We had to fly the army into Montreal. Cabinet ministers, the Prime Minister, the then leader of the opposition and all other official people in Ottawa had to be protected by army officers. Those officers were armed with particularly fast guns with hair-triggers. Was this government trying to tell us that it was against treason and that it did not believe in capital punishment when there was only the slightest tremor? This House has heard no evidence to suggest it was anything more that the slightest tremor. The

July 5, 1976

Rose brothers and a couple of others looked all over the United States for a couple of guns, and kidnapped two important people in Montreal. There was a so-called armed insurrection against the government-that is what we were told in this House, and we have heard nothing since.
An abolitionist cabinet immediately conned the rest of the House of Commons into believing that we were faced with an armed insurrection and that officers had to be armed and flown in from all over Canada to protect officials wherever they might be in Ottawa or Montreal. Was that not an expression of a deliberate preparedness to use capital punishment as a deterrent to the continuance of that so-called insurrection against Canada and the government? To me it was. Surely the government of the day must have thought that people were prepared to commit treason as defined in this clause. That is what we were told people in the FLQ were prepared to do. The FLQ was banned, and that is still the case. That is the only time in Canada's peacetime that an organization has been banned.
Many people over the past 30 or so years have often talked about banning the Communist party, but that has never come about. The Communist party exists, holds meetings and fields candidates in general elections, but because of this supposed threat the FLQ was banned. I point this out to suggest that this government in the past was prepared to use the death penalty when it felt that treason was being committed. I am not suggesting that in cases such as that nearly everyone caught-the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) shakes his head in a negative manner: If I am misinterpreting-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: You are.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The minister suggests that I am. He is permitted to get up after I have finished and straighten me out. I will listen to him.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
However, his government has yet to put the facts on the table and to prove that there was an armed insurrection. Were those army officers, who were armed with guns, prepared to use them? Yes, they were. The record of this House is that they were issued with special guns and were specially trained soldiers. The guns were equipped with hair-triggers. I know what a hair-trigger is and that those guns were so equipped, because at that time an officer shot himself getting out of a truck outside my apartment. I know very well how they were armed and the type of hair-trigger on those guns. The government was prepared to use the death penalty for what it thought was treason, without giving people a fair trial. Over 400 people were arrested, all of whom were released and very few, if any, were charged. Why am I raising this matter, Mr. Speaker? It is merely to point out that this government acknowledges that when they feel threatened themselves, they will resort to the worst kind of use of capital punishment.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson) spoke about the recent terrorist incident in Uganda and the build-up of terrorism throughout the world. We can be fairly proud of our country as we have been relatively free
Capital Punishment
of acts of international terrorism since 1972. But surely we must not be so complacent as to rest on our laurels and do away with the one measure which is a forceful deterrent. Some hon. members hide behind the belief that it has not been proven that it is a deterrent. It is a deterrent, Mr. Speaker. A deterrent is in the eyes of the person attempting to commit a crime. If 80 per cent of the people of the country believe it is a deterrent, then it is.
There is no question that the kidnappers of James Cross believed they might be shot if an exchange of gunfire took place between them and the police. A great deal of caution was taken in what might even be considered the preliminary negotiations when anonymous notes were dropped off at a radio station, and so on. They went to a great deal of trouble to keep the negotiations at more than arm's length because they were fearful for their lives. That suggests to me that those who kidnapped James Cross believed that the death penalty was a deterrent The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre suggested that Her Majesty has not requested it. Certainly, I believe that in many instances Her Majesty would extend clemency to those whose who made an attempt on her life.
Another thing should be mentioned in regard to treason, Mr. Speaker. Murder is committed by those who deliberately attempt to take the life of another. Treason is committed by a person or persons deliberately acting against the wish of the government or, in this case, the wish of Her Majesty or against the country. But the law should be fair and equal to all, and the death penalty for treason should be applicable to all, whether they be rich or poor. It is the duty of the courts to administer it fairly and apply it equally. It is the duty of the legislators to make the law and to amend the law, and it is the duty of the courts to apply it equally. Certainly, those with hope will use every avenue available to them before their hope is exhausted. Those without hope, I suppose, will resign themselves to what they consider the inevitable, in any case.
I sincerely urge this House, at this time in Canada's history, when it is faced with an overwhelming desire of the Canadian people to see retention of capital punishment, an overwhelming desire of the Canadian people to see a successful and harmonious execution of the Olympic games, and an overwhelming desire of the Canadian people to see that justice not only appear to be done but is in fact done, to delete clause 2 from the bill. If it is deleted and the bill carries, then capital punishment will apply to those people who have been proven to have either killed or attempted to kill Her Majesty, who have levied war against Canada or have used force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada.
I am simplifying the three major clauses, Mr. Speaker. This law would only be applied if it were proven that a person committed such an act or was a party to committing such an act. That is of the utmost importance, because I am certain that anybody involved in the least way in threatening the life or security of a cabinet minister during the October crisis would not have had a fair trial under this government. He probably would not even have had a chance to go to court. In fact, he probably would have been 
shot. There is the irony of this same government now coming forward with a bill to delete a fair trial for an act of treason.
However, if somewhere down the road members of the government desire to call in the armed forces again at the flick of a television camera by saying that an armed insurrection is arising and they must call in the troops to deal with those attemping to overthrow the government, they are permitted to do that. The passage of this bill will not prohibit the government from doing that without first proving to parliament and the country that there are forces attempting to overthrow the government. That is the sham of this abolitionist cabinet. Its members want to do away with justice and take the law into their own hands.
This cabinet says we do not need the death penalty for treason, just leave it to them. If they think someone is trying to overthrow the government, they will not bother with a trial. They will call in the army. That is the injustice of clause 2 of this legislation.
There is supposed to be a free vote on this legislation. I therefore urge all members of parliament, including those on the government side, to think seriously about this. By supporting this amendment they will not defeat the bill. In fact it will probably result in the Olympics running a little smoother. The bill would then allow Canada to be governed a little more smoothly. Mr. Speaker, I too rise in support of my colleague's amendment which proposes that clause 2 of Bill C-84 be deleted, the net effect being to preserve the treason provisions that now exist in our Criminal Code.
Frankly I am quit surprised to hear people who have taken part in this debate state this afternoon that they do not understand what treason is. They ask for the definition of treason.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) seemed to be confused about what the government is doing through Bill C-84, namely, attempting to make us not just an abolitionist state by law for ordinary crimes, but attempting to make us an abolitionist state in total. I say that because it has become a kind of Liberal misrepresentation that the world is gravitating toward abolition, that somehow or other Canada is out of step with the rest of the world by not being an abolitionist nation along with what they fancy is desirable. As we stated in the House and in committee, that is absolutely wrong. It is a falsehood.
At the present time, the vast majority of the nations of the world are retentionist nations. In fact if we pass Bill C-84 in its present form we will become part of 1 per cent of the world's population that lives in a state that is in effect totally abolitionist. Surely it is us who will be out of step with the world, not the reverse which the government is indicating. I mention this because in committee the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) made a point of stating that democracies in the western world are taking to abolition as opposed to the retentionist traditions. I pointed this out to the committee. Even if one takes into account nations such as the United Kingdom, which have limited the use of the death penalty, one finds they did not limit the death penalty with regard to treason. This is one of the reasons for .which I believe the amendment by my hon. friend is well worthy of consideration.
I should like to give briefly a little of the background to show where this concept of treason as an offence originated. This was an offence in Roman times, and is one of the most fundamental concepts of criminal law in existence. I would refer hon. members to the 1973 edition of the Encyclopedia Britannica where it is stated that treason is the crime of betraying the nation or its sovereign by acts considered dangerous to their security. The article states that among most nations from very early times the punishment for treason has been severe. Death has been the mandatory sentence in England, and that provision was
Capital Punishment
not affected by the limitation on the application of the death penalty effected by that country a few years ago.
That is the first point I wish to make. We have been told repeatedly by the government that we were somehow introducing into our own penal system laws which already existed in countries such as the United Kingdom. That is not true if we include the treason provisions contemplated in Bill C-84. The Encyclopedia goes on to say:
The law of England regarding treason corresponds to a considerable extent to Roman law ... The offence of high treason was not precisely defined by the common law until the passing of the Treason Act in 1351.
So the section of the Criminal Code we are today proposing to do away with-irresponsibly, I suggest-is one which has been in our criminal law as far as Britain is concerned since 1351. And in the eyes of the British courts the statute of 1351, so far as it defines the offence of high treason, is still law.
I refer to Britain because, of course, most of our common law and criminal law come from that country. But take the practice in the United States. The crime of treason was written right into the constitution by its framers back in 1776.

In section 3(3) treason is defined in the United States constitution, and in section 3(2) it is stated that Congress shall have the power to determine the punishment for treason. It is interesting to note that U.S. criminal law states that whoever, owing allegiance to the United States, levies war against them or adheres to their enemies ... is guilty of treason and shall suffer death. There are other alternative sentences provided. So that is the practice in the two countries to which we traditionally look-the United States, our neighbour, and Great Britain from which we derive the bulk of our criminal and common law.
Speaking of the United States, I am sure no one in this House will have failed to note the judgment which came down from the U.S. Supreme Court making it clear-there has been some doubt-that the death penalty is not to be held as contrary to the constitution of that country. I am curious to know whether the Solicitor General took time this week end to read the judgment which was handed down in Washington because it is timely as far as Canada is concerned. I hope every hon. member who retains the wishy-washy impression that somehow or other the Americans are tending to favour an abolitionist state will read that judgment and note what some of the judges of the U.S. Supreme Court say about the use of the death penalty in the system of criminal law.
What is happening in the United States? The fact is that the death penalty there has been extended, not lessened, contrary to misleading statements sometimes made by government members in support of this bill. I should like to refer to some of the statements which were made in the course of that judgment by the U.S. Supreme Court. The court made it clear that the death penalty was a constitutional penalty and should not be considered otherwise, and further that its imposition could be left in the hands of judges or jurors.

Capital Punishment
Perhaps I should comment that this ruling was the first on the death penalty since June 29, 1972, when it ruled by five to four that the law then on the books gave too much discretion to judges and juries. That decision invalidated death penalty laws of 36 states, the District of Columbia and of the federal government. In the aftermath of the 1972 decision, 35 states re-enacted the death penalty, but in one of them, Illinois, the law was struck down by the state's Supreme Court. The U.S. Supreme Court, in its judgment, said the enactment of capital punishment by state legislatures was "a marked indication of society's endorsement of the death penalty for murder."
When this question came up in committee I was surprised to find the Solicitor General unaware that while there were 13 abolitionist states at the time he introduced his last abolitionist or partial abolitionist legislation in this House, there are only ten today. He had to correct himself. He was not aware of this until he was so advised by his officials. Opinion in the United States has been reversing itself in the two or three years during which the minister has been attempting to make Canada an abolitionist nation.
It might be helpful, in considering whether the death penalty for treason should remain, to consider the differences in outlook between our Solicitor General and that of the solicitor general of the United States. The Solicitor General of Canada and the solicitor general of the United States are charged with a similar duty, that of upholding the law, yet both have such divergent views. For example, the solicitor general of the United States had this to say:

The United States believes that imposition of the death penalty may sometimes be a necessary and appropriate measure to achieve the traditional goals of criminal justice ...
He points out that, following the 1972 decision I have referred to, Congress enacted a statute providing the death penalty for aircraft piracy that results in death. Again the solicitor general of the United States, in sharp contrast to the weak-kneed approach of our Solicitor General, at page 5 of his brief said that the death penalty is a traditional sanction for those offences society considers the most dangerous. He went on in his very extensive brief to express the view that capital punishment serves other purposes as well. He said:
The death penalty serves a vital function as society's expression of moral outrage, and marks off some crimes as so repulsive that they are to be avoided by those individuals with even a trace of social responsibility. Some crimes, too, are so vicious, so offensive to society's standards of decency, that they call out for an ultimate sanction in order to reinforce the social feeling of revulsion to acts of that character. This response-retribution perhaps, although without vindictiveness-has been endorsed by respected commentators and seems an essential ingredient of a healthy society.
I am quoting directly from the brief of the United States solicitor general submitted to the Supreme Court of the United States, which court in turn held substantially in favour of his representation. The U.S. solicitor general continued:
Finally, capital punishment incapacitates some individuals who, if allowed to remain alive, would be so immune to normal forms of social control that they would continue to commit murders even if sentenced to life imprisonment without possibility of parole. The federal prison system now confines at least one man who, since his incarceration for
(Mr. Stevens.]
murder, has committed and been convicted of murders within prison on three separate occasions.
How often has it been pointed out in this House, Mr. Speaker, that if a man is sentenced to prison for life for committing murder, what is to prevent him from murdering a second or third time? The U.S. solicitor general makes that very point. He says that there is at least one person in the United States who, on three separate occasions, has committed murder after being sentenced to life imprisonment. He continued:
This man, and others like him, will find opportunities to kill again, regardless of the care taken to guard them ...
Although there may be legitimate differences of opinion regarding capital punishment's acceptance by modern society, its value as a deterrent, and society's need for it to reinforce social values and incapacitate dangerous offenders, those differences of opinion are to be resolved by the legislature; and the legislative judgment on these matters should be accepted by the judicial arm.
I could quote many similar portions of the U.S. solicitor general's submission, but I wish only to highlight the sharp contrast between the present trend in the United States in terms of retaining and even extending the death penalty and Bill C-84, if it should finally pass this House-heaven forbid. The reason I raise these points is to preserve the fundamental view that a crime such as treason, which I have defined for the House, is at least one crime for which any person found guilty should expect to pay with his life.
I suggest that we were right today to indicate our approval for the effective and speedy action taken by the government of Israel in rescuing refugees from the terrorists who held them in Uganda.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to speak to the amendment to clause 2 dealing with treason and high treason. I think for the record it would be interesting to members, particularly those opposite, to have an indication of what countries have abolished capital punishment in its entirety and what countries have abolished capital punishment by law for only the ordinary crime of murder.
I should like to indicate that Austria, Columbia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Equador, Finland, the Federal Republic of Germany, Iceland, Sweden, Uruguay, and Venezuela are all countries which have abolished the death penalty. The remaining countries provide the death penalty for treason. I think it is also interesting to note that with the exception of three of four of these countries the

majority are in the southern hemisphere, South America, Latin America or Central America. I shall not embarrass the countries by naming them specifically, but surely the diplomats, the consuls and the ambassadors know to which countries I allude. These countries have their own forms of capital punishment which, to the people of the democratic or free world, are repugnant. Whether capital punishment be carried out by black boots or brown boots according to the philosophy of the country, nevertheless it is still enforced.
I believe that unquestionably throughout the world we have entered into a period of change in the thinking of nations which at times, in my view, borders on madness, perhaps brought about by extreme degrees of frustration and, in some instances, suppression. Nevertheless we have seen the advent of a new time, a new era, throughout the world when countries are divided, with despots seeking the platform on some popular public issue and carrying a country on a wave of independence, only subsequently to rule that country with an iron fist. This bears on one thing. It bears on the absence of tradition.
I suppose any nation has a tradition, but the true, deep-seated, ingrained definition of tradition, that lies in the hearts particularly of Canadians and people associated with Great Britain or her dominions, is not easily dispelled. I know that today in Canada there are those who speak with scorn about Her Majesty, and yet there are thousands upon thousands of Canadians who fought for Her Majesty and who refer to her with admiration.

I ask every member of the House to ponder on what kind of a television appearance the Prime Minister would make if he were to announce that at the Olympics some mad dog of an assassin attempted or succeeded in killing the Queen. What would that type of horrible tragedy do to this nation? Would it tear us apart? It would certainly tear us apart as far as our hearts are concerned.
You may say, you are just thinking in terms of revenge if you are going to hang the individual concerned, if the crowd did not tear him asunder first. Most nations have from early times provided for the punishment of treason. Punishment has characterically been severe .. . death is still the mandatory sentence-

I am concerned with my view and those supporting it. If hon. members opposite have something to say that they think is constructive, I think it befits them to join the debate. Either put up or shut up.
The subject of treason has been one that has been brought forward at the United Nations, because it is a separate and distinct entity. How did the U.N. agonize over the issue? In a review by the United Nations on the current situation the following was stated:
In academic circles it has sometimes become unfashionable to support capital punishment: civilization is tolerance and severity in punishment a sign of backwardness and regression, and so liberal thinking and the abolition of the death penalty are expected to coincide. Therefore the writing available on the death penalty leaves the impression that there is a certain inevitability about the movement to more "civilized standards" and fewer executions. A reader could be excused for concluding that throughout the world there is in fact an irresistible and ineluctable trend towards the abolition of capital punishment or that even where death is still a last legal resort, the penal codes have fewer offences leading to capital punishment or that methods of execution are becoming more humane or that the persons liable to the extreme penalty will usually have the benefit of the best legal safeguards.
The world at present provides no such assurances. Moreover it seems clear that in many cases governments satisfy public opinion by using the sentence, but no so in Canada. There is evidence that even the countries totally abolishing capital punishment have sometimes, if not always, acted contrary to the majority view of the population. However, that is nothing new for this government, and I do not care whether those on the opposite side would like to say that they have the opportunity to vote freely. I shall never forget that date when I watched the Prime Minister sit there as he has never sat there before through any vote, and swivel his head back and forth like a tortoise or an owl. Mr. Speaker, thank you for advising the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain that he did not have a valid point of order. I certainly agree with you that this is nothing unusual for that member.
Let me continue my remarks with regard to the position taken by the U.S. government. The United States believes that the imposition of the death penalty may sometimes be a necessity and an appropriate measure to achieve the traditonal goals of criminal justice. Congress enacted a statute providing the death penalty for aircraft piracy that results in death. How many hon. members recall the incident over Canada's air space when those murderers who kill for profit caused an aircraft to blow up, taking many lives with it? What happened to them? I clearly remember without any regret that they paid the supreme penalty.
The government would have us believe that those who are prepared to destroy the lives of 100, 200 or 300 people in one fell swoop by blowing up an aircraft, can be rehabilitated, and I ask: rehabilitated to what, to kill again? The statistics are there; the minister has his own statistics, and I have read them. The facts are there, that certainly murderers who have been released have murdered again. Why should that be allowed to happen? Particularly with regard to crimes against the state and crimes against the sovereign, this should not be allowed to happen. Does the government condone the action of some mad dog who would commit treason?
Let me warn hon. members that I am aware of the fine line between sedition and treason. I am aware of the definition, and I am aware of the difference between espionage and treason, but these things do exist, and on the basis of present day technology they are highly possible. Hon. members tell me that 25 years, 10 years or 7 years will rehabilitate the mad dog who, with full foreknowledge of his action and with every degree of premeditation he can summon, sets out to murder Canadians through an act of treason, or sets out to murder the sovereign. Do hon. members think that the penalty should be a few years in jail and that he would then be rehabilitated?
Speaking of tradition, I must say thank God the tradition in Canada, at least thus far, has not been to shoot presidents or prime ministers. Tradition in the United States would certainly seem to be the contrary, and from an examination of those who have committed this horrible act, the majority of them have paid the supreme penalty. It is only in the more enlightened days of the immediate past that we have seen attacks on presidential candidates not lead eventually to that supreme penalty.
On behalf of all those Canadians who have risen with one voice, either through the medium of the press, through the medium of writing to their MLA's and their members of parliament, through the medium of hotlines or whatever medium, I say that by a vast majority they have indicated

July 5, 1976

that they have been treacherously dealt with by the government, and that they consider that members of parliament who represent them here and who do not carry out the wishes of their constituents are demonstrating a failure to respond to the demands and views of Canadians.
I have no difficulty with my conscience on this issue at all. Not only do I support the wishes of my constituents, but it should be clearly elucidated and pretty well a matter of fact, and there should be no doubt in the minds of those here tonight, that my position fully supports the fact that the amendment with reference to treason should stand, that the supreme penalty should be paid as far as treason is concerned, and that this clause should be removed from the bill and dealt with as a separate entity.

Mr. Speaker, motions Nos. 7 and 10 highlight two clauses of Bill C-84 which caused me the other day to make an observation, that is on June 29 when Mr. Speaker was considering whether there was a central principle to Bill C-84, it being the abolition of capital punishment. At that time I suggested that that was not the case, and further reading of the bill has convinced me that I was right at that time. There has been a failure to appreciate one single fact with regard to Bill C-84. It is an amending bill, and all an amending bill does is amend a number of sections in existing law which themselves each embody a principle. Then there is the central theme in a total bill-new legislation. That aspect of Bill C-84 has been lost sight of. It is a bill to amend the Criminal Code. That is its principle.
When one considers clause 2 of the bill, there is created there a totally new offence, high treason. What has that got to do with the so-called central theme of the abolition of capital punishment in this bill? All the clauses which follow with regard to parole following life sentences are already dealt with under the Criminal Code, but the terms of parole thereunder are being changed. Is the central theme the abolition of capital punishment? Hardly. Therefore I am glad to participate in this debate, but I underline those arguments.
I accept Mr. Speaker's ruling. I listened to it, I must conform to it, but that does not mean I must agree with it, and I respectfully draw to the attention of the Chair this particular aspect of my remarks.
Let us look at sections 46 and 47 of the Criminal Code. Treason is dealt with in section 46, and there are eight paragraphs enumerated there which constitute treason and have constituted treason in the history of Canada much longer than you, Mr. Speaker, and I have been around. But now, for some fanciful reason, three types of treason are to be elevated to high treason, and one of the forms under section 46(1) is being totally eliminated. I wonder why? I ask the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) why it is that conspiracy to kill Her Majesty should not be high treason if the killing, the attempting to kill or doing bodily harms is to be high treason? It was formerly part of treason. It was dealt with in section 46(l)(d). However, that has disappeared in the shuffle of setting up high treason and, I suppose, second class treason. We now have this treason affecting the life and the person of the reigning monarch.

Then there is the second question of levying war against Canada or doing any act preparatory thereto, but why would not conspiracy to do that be part of it? Is the only one who actually is levying the war the one who will be guilty of high treason? Are his partners-and I say "his" in the general sense-to escape entirely? That is not a crime under the new bill.
The third category is assisting an enemy at war with Canada, or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities whether or not a state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are. High treason? Well, the wording is the same as the first three paragraphs of what it was for treason, so what is new? It has been made high treason. That is the principle of the amending clause. It has nothing to do with capital punishment.
Then we deal with every one who commits treason, and we have the paragraphs broken down. In section 46.(1)(/) of the Criminal Code it provides that everyone commits treason who:
conspires with any person to do anything mentioned in paragraphs (a) to (d);
We had a whole series of forms of treason where there was also conspiracy which in itself was treason, but it is no longer there. At worst it is treason to conspire with a person to commit high treason. I find it extraordinary that to conspire with a person to commit high treason is simply treason. The Solicitor General has a great deal to answer for a regard to setting up this section and the wording of it.

When I was a student whether in high school or at university one of the things that was emphasized to us was confinement to the Bastille by lettre de cachet. In other words it was possible to be banished for life into the confines of the Bastille. These provisions, Mr. Speaker, are the equivalent of lettre de cachet, although I suppose the physical conditions have changed. There will be better food and better accommodation than in the Bastille there is no doubt, but there is not guarantee that another prisoner or prisoners will not murder within the prison. Perhaps the state wants it that way, as I speculated the other day.
There was another type of punishment that was always emphasized to us as the most heinous that man could inflict upon his fellowman. That was a life sentence to

Devil's Island. That was at least 25 years. As I said the other day on second reading, we have devised our own sadistic torture of our fellowman. Has anyone here contemplated what 25 years in prison can do?
