The hon. member demonstrates a craven subservience to the views of leadership-the present views of his leader on this particular subject. The other day it was apparent in the debate, and it is apparent today.
We have this sentence of 25 years for high treason, ten years certain for treason, and the judge may impose an additional period. I think there are inconsistencies here. Why should there be any difference between an attempt to kill the reigning monarch and a violent attempt to overthrow the lawful authority of the state? Why would there be any difference between assisting an enemy during a time of war-that is someone performing that act outside the country-and someone inside carrying on a guerilla command?
One is guilty of high treason if, sitting on the Islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, one were to discharge long range firearms at the coast of Newfoundland, but if within the province of Newfoundland one were to discharge those self-same guns in order to upset the government of Newfoundland or the power of the Government of Canada, that would simply be treason. Can anyone in their right senses explain the difference? Who shall be the more guilty-he who stands on the shore of St. Pierre and Miquelon and fires at the coast of Newfoundland, or he who stands within a few miles of St. John's and fires the same gun at St. John's? This is treason and high treason-an act of war. I shall let my colleagues figure that one out a little later.
I am more than satisfied that my colleagues who put forward these amendments are correct-the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). I think they highlight a most important and a very substantial amendment to the Criminal Code. Incidentally, it drags in by the tail the question of capital punishment. It is only consequential on the division of the crimes. Therefore I am more than happy to support both motions, Nos. 7 and 10. I think it is an illogical mishmash in so far as all those treasonable acts that have existed in the past are concerned and which are now supposedly being redefined in some sort of modern
Capital Punishment
context which exists in the mind of the draftsman alone. His logic and that of the sponsors escapes most people. Therefore I would ask all members of this House to delete clause 2.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before speaking on the amendment this evening I wish to congratulate our American friends on their decision just a few days ago in which their Supreme Court upheld the death penalty. I have an article here headed "Supreme Court Decision on Death Penalty Hailed". I quote:
The Supreme Court is thinking like the American people are thinking," said a state senator from Maine.
It is unfortunate that this House is not thinking like the Canadian people are thinking.
And there was little doubt the court ruling upholding the concept of capital punishment for murders brings the court a lot closer to the thinking of most Americans.
I wish I were reading that it was bringing our courts closer to the thinking of most Canadians. However, that will not happen with this government.
Unfortunately many members of the opposition, especially NDP members who are supposed to be the champions of the people, are totally opposed to what the majority of Canadians want. I find this very strange.
I will read to hon. members the law as it is now so that there will be no mistake about it. This law has been on the statute book for years. I quote the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who saw the weaknesses in this bill probably better than any other member. He is to be commended for the research he has done into this piece of legislation. I quote:
The Canadian Civil Liberties Organization has not asked that the law regarding treason be repealed. Again I challenge the government to name one organization or anyone of responsibility across Canada who has asked for this. The sections in question should be placed on the record. Sections 46 and 47 at present read as follows:
46(1) Every one commits treason who, in Canada
(a)	kills or attempts to kill'Her Majesty, or does her any bodily harm tending to death or destruction, maims or wounds her, or imprisons or restrains her;
(b)	levies war against Canada or does any act preparatory thereto;
(c)	assists an enemy at war with Canada, or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities . ..
(d)	uses force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada or a province;
(e)	without lawful authority, communicates or makes available to an agent of a state other than Canada, military or scientific information or any sketch, plan, model, article, note or document of a military or scientific character that he knows or ought to know may be used by that state for a purpose prejudicial to the safety or defence of Canada .. .
47(1) Every one who commits treason is guilty of an indictable
offence and is liable
(a) To be sentenced to death if he is guilty of an offence under paragraph 46(l)(a), (b) or (c)-
That is the killing or the attempted killing of the Queen of Canada, to levy war against Canada or to assist an enemy at war with Canada. Why has this been changed at this time? Nobody has answered that. Again I repeat: there is something gratuitous about the government's action in this regard. Then so far as penalties are concerned, if all one does is to use force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the

July 5, 1976
Capital Punishment
government of Canada or a province, they may be sentenced to death or to imprisonment for life.
There is something behind this, and that is what we have not found out. What has activated the government of Canada to bring before the House legislation which will make Canada an open place for assassination and treason subject only to a jail sentence in a world in which terrorism marches and assassinations and kidnappings with assassination take place all over the world? Just at this time the Government of Canada decides that it must be kind to terrorists, international murders and those who raise rebellion.
The only government member who has entered into the debate in the past few days has talked in defence of a number of charges contained in letters to Hamilton newspapers. It is unfortunate that he has not expounded on capital punishment because of the two different stands he has taken on it. It would be a great contribution if he would expound on this issue. I see he has left the Chamber. Possibly later this evening the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) will expand on the two different stands he has taken with regard to capital punishment.
As I stated earlier, they have brought back capital punishment in the United States. A number of states have passed laws bringing back capital punishment. I wish to go into a bit of the history and the reasons why the United States has brought it back.
In 1965 New York abolished capital punishment except for someone convicted of killing a peace officer acting in the line of duty, and for a life convict who murders a guard or inmate in prison or while attempting to escape. The same year Vermont abandoned the death penalty except for treason, kidnapping for ransom, and for those who have been convicted of murder in the first degree and commit a second "unrelated" murder and for those convicts who murder any employee of the state prison or house of correction or a person known by the offender to be a law-enforcement officer performing the duties of his office.
I presume all hon. members received today the latest communication from the Public Service Alliance of Canada. It is addressed to "Honourable Members of the House of Commons". It points out the concern of our prison guards. These guards could soon be looking after prisoners convicted of treason. With the Olympics coming up, we can expect just about anything. Enclosed with the letter is a full statement on their concerns for their lives and the lack of protection in our prisons today. They state, and I quote:
Please find attached a copy of a paper presented to the Solicitor General of Canada, Honourable Warren Allmand, in his office on June 29, 1976.
In our closing paragraph to the Solicitor General of Canada we have requested that this bill be tabled until he is able to provide a special institution to ensure the security and safety of all penitentiary personnel working in institutions.
Of course the answer we will receive from the government with regard to dealing with murderers is that it will build smaller, more comfortable jails. That is not the answer.
We humbly urge you on behalf of all penitentiary personnel and their families to defeat Bill C-84, otherwise you will have to bear the responsibility that will ensue from the chaotic situation that will result from your negative vote on the security of all law abiding citizens of Canada.

This is the second document I have received from prison guards in the last ten days. They go into explicit detail concerning the problems they are experiencing. This brings me back to my original speech on capital punishment in which I suggested that the abolitionists might change places with the guards and take responsibility for looking after Mad Dog Kelly and other ruthless killers of his type, men you cannot turn your back on for one second. If hon. members want to learn in detail what it is like to look after individuals of his sort I suggest they contact some jail guards.
In the United States there are certain crimes against government and there are two crimes in particular which fall into this category, treason and perjury. Our concern today arises from the proposal to drop the penalty of capital punishment with respect to treason. Treason is the act of levying war against the government of a jurisdiction or of giving aid and comfort to its enemies. Twenty jurisdictions punish treason with death. Twelve of them demand death on conviction-there is no alternative sentence. This places treason third in the rank order of offences punishable by death and first in the rank order of mandatory sentences.
Also there are crimes against property which can become capital. They include train wrecking, arson and burglary. I should like to add another crime-that of hijacking. I am reminded of a case in San Francisco a couple of years ago. A retired couple were on a United States jet aircraft which was taken over by hijackers. There was an exchange of gunfire within the aircraft and the husband was killed before the eyes of the wife. He was down in the States looking for a place for retirement. I find it very strange that abolitionists would want to deal so leniently with hijackers. Fortunately, in this case, the two hijackers were killed by FBI agents when they left the aircraft. But our Canadian retired railway worker lay in the aircraft in a pool of blood.
Train wrecking is generally any act such as tampering with switches or signals or burning trestles with intent to derail a train. In most jurisdictions the offence becomes capital only if someone dies as a result of such wrecking. Eighteen jurisdictions provide the death penalty for train wrecking; three of them make death mandatory.
Arson is the wilful and malicious burning of the building of another. Georgia, for example, has six arson statutes all making arson a capital crime. Four of them make arson imputed murder if death occurs as a result. Arson is ninth in the rank order of offences with nine jurisdictions punishing it. There are no mandatory jurisdiction. The death penalty in relation to all these crimes is being removed and those who commit them will simply receive a nice life sentence in a comfortable jail in return for these very serious offences.
With regard to the relation between the law, crime, and executions, let me say that anyone who hopes to understand the place of capital punishment in contemporary American society must have a grasp of the latest information on at least four aspects of this subject. First, he needs to know what crimes in each American jurisdiction are at present punishable by death. Next, he needs to know how many of each of these crimes actually occur. Third, he
July 5, 1976

must understand the scope of liability for a death sentence, especially as juveniles are affected. Lastly, he should have some idea of the ultimate fate of a typical group of persons originally sentenced to death by reference to a record of those who have been executed.
It is probable that few Americans have any idea how many crimes still carry a death penalty-anywhere from 33 to 67 crimes depending on how they are classified. They range from familiar ones such as murder, kidnapping, rape, and treason, to such crimes as desecrating a grave (Georgia), attempting to set fire to a prison (Arkansas), and sexually assaulting a girl under 18-so-called "statutory rape" (Nevada and Texas). Just in the past week there has been another violent rape and murder of a nine-year-old girl in British Columbia. The answer to this is apparently to build smaller and more comfortable jails in which to look after these criminals. I know the Canadian people will not accept this.
What do Americans think of the death penalty today? Their attitudes obviously govern the likelihood of retaining, extending or abolishing it in that country in our time. In 1964 Governor George E. Chamberlain, in his inaugural address to the legislature, recommended that all executions should take place within the walls of a penitentiary. In the same year a law was passed requiring that all executions take place at the state penitentiary at Salem, and two years later Governor Chamberlain said he was sure this law would be most beneficial in its results.
Just before closing, I should like to make a brief comment. A 25-year-old youth from Winnipeg, the city from which I come, was found dead in the streets of New Orleans as last week. He had been knifed to death by a mugger. Murder on the streets is becoming almost a daily event, and the majority of Canadians are demanding that we return to capital punishment. We should bow to their wishes. I have conducted two polls in my riding which show that 80 per cent want the retention of capital punishment. And one poll carried out this year shows that 90 per cent want capital punishment retained.
I hear an intervention by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain to whom I referred earlier in my speech. I hope he will explain to us tonight why he has taken two different stands on this question of capital punishment. I believe he owes us some explanation, not just a brief interjection such as he made last Wednesday. I think it might prove to be an excellent contribution, one which would help us understand the two different stances he has taken.

This has been manifested in a strange and unpredictable way, through this issue that is known as bilingualism in the air. It in itself belies a far more serious problem. It tells us that what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said some weeks ago regarding those who would cause Canada to end as a nation is simply wishful thinking, is not true.
There do exist organized forces in this land prepared and ready to do our country in, to end Canada. We know now that we cannot hide from that awful fact any longer. We must be prepared to face the dire consequences that may be caused by the actions of those individuals and groups. The lesson of terrorism has been brought home to us this very day in the wake of the situation in the Middle East. There we saw an example of why the penalty for terrorism, treason and acts of piracy, which will be dealt with in another amendment similar to this, should be and, indeed, must be kept in the law.
I would ask you why those guerrillas hijacked the plane and held those innocent people captive? It was for the purpose of freeing other people who had committed political crimes, crimes of terrorism and crimes of air piracy, yet because they had not paid the penalty for these heinous crimes they were still alive in jail providing sufficient motivation to these people to commit this terrible act. They played with those people's lives so they could spring from prison their associates and accomplices in international crime.
I submit to you that the same type of devious mentality is open to committing the crime of treason. If we just lock up so-called political prisoners after they have tried to take the life of the nation, we make heroes of them to that small sect in society. What do we offer these people and their accomplices who are still on the outside and have not yet been arrested? We offer them a reason and an opportunity to commit more crime by holding other people hostage and by performing other acts of terrorism only to push forward this demented cause.
As never before, the future of this country is on the minds and in the hearts of hon. members and all Canadians. I came to Ottawa, to Parliament Hill, in 1972 prior to the general election of that year as executive assistant to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker). I did not know at that time, nor in the years I was at school and knew him through correspondence and occasional visits, that we would ever have the opportunity of sitting together in parliament. To me that seemed an unreachable goal and a dream that just could not be realized. Following the election of October 1972 an unusual set of circumstances allowed me to come into this House and sit as a colleague of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert and that was an honour given me by the people of Hamilton-Wentworth that no words can adequately express.
The right hon. gentleman and I have been associated for many years. As I said, prior to coming into this House I worked on his staff. We have not always agreed, and he has never asked me to always agree with him. He has often told me that his outlook in this House and in a lifetime of politics is that strong men have strong opinions, that they are bound to disagree, but that should not interfere with the maintenance and growth of their friendship. That is how it has been with us. His record here, before the courts,
Capital Punishment
and in all his public life has been that of an unswerving abolitionist. He has said so in this House. His contribution to this country is unmatched in our lifetime. He now places before us the value of his experience. It is something to all hon. members, be they retentionists such as myself, or abolitionists by nature, such as the right hon. member for Prince Albert, and, worth bearing in mind.
He has told us that on the basis of his experience as Prime Minister of this country and as a private member that, while he still favours abolition, he would not and could not support a bill that would contribute to the demise of this country by doing away with the right of the state to impose capital punishment for the commission of the crime of treason.
Let me conclude my remarks with a non-partisan appeal to all members, be they abolitionists or retentionists, to support the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta, and be consistent. There is no difficulty in doing that. I say to all of them, through you, Sir, that we would all like to live in a kind of world of which we dream, and the kind of world we came here to work for, but we dare not confuse that kind of world with a dream world, a world that still eludes us and is not here and will not be here if we capitulate to the forces of international terrorism. That world will continue to elude us if we. open up this country to the heinous crimes that can be committed, indeed, it is sad to say, would be encouraged by leaving out this right of society. That kind of world will elude us as long as those forces are at work. They are at work today, and it is about time we got to work to make sure that the people of Canada are protected and that the future of Canada is ensured, by supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move this motion for the purpose of deleting clause 3 of Bill C-84. I should like now to explain this motion and the reasons which warrant it.
Section 75(2) of the Criminal Code, notwithstanding the provisions of Bill C-84, states:
(2) Every one who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life, but. ..
And it is this part of the quotation which the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has struck out:
. .. but if while committing or attempting to commit piracy he murders or attemps to murder another person or does any act that is likely to endanger the life of another person he shall be sentenced to death."
Such was the section of the Criminal Code in effect in Canada. The Solicitor General proposes in Bill C-84 that the clause that I have just quoted be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
(2) Every one who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that the Solicitor General by including a clause on piracy in his bill recognized that it is a kind of crime and therefore recognized its existence. In committee, before the end of the proceedings, the minister said that there had been no crime of piracy in Canada since 1900 and that consequently it was not necessary to include it in our bill.
Mr. Speaker, what seems to motivate the Solicitor General is that it is a crime. It was in the Criminal Code. It might look bad to abolish it completely. There has been no such crime in Canada since 1900. It is not that serious and we are going to include it to appease the conscience of Canadians. Then, piracy is still a crime but we will eliminate the penalty provided for attempted murder or premeditated murder.
Mr. Speaker, for this minister, piracy is not a crime punishable by death. I wish to draw the attention of my colleagues on that. What is an act of piracy? Is it the kind of pirate stories we had in the Middle Ages? Everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, that it is not that. Modern piracy is when an individual or a group of individuals decide to take hold of a private or public transportation means. It might be an airplane, a train, a boat or a bus. A group of criminals

takes over that transportation means in a systematic, premeditated, organized way and while doing it, they endanger the lives of passengers.
Mr. Speaker, it is then a serious situation. It is a mordern phenomenon. The minister said before the committee that it has not happened since 1900 and consequently, it was not really serious. Is it necessary, Mr. Speaker, to have it happen just once and that fifty people be treatened, held hostages on any transportation means in Canada and that there be many victims for the minister to open his eyes and recognize that it is a modern act?
The minister suggested in committee that it was an outdated crime that was no longer committed in our modern times. Well, as everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, there are hijackings, piracy acts in which citizens are held hostages, acts such as what took place in Montreal, some time ago, where a criminal seized a school bus and held children-not adults but children-hostages and threatened them, because he wanted something in return and therefore, he resorted to blackmail, using children's lives, and it happened in the city of Montreal in 1976.
This is therefore a serious and modern act which must be treated seriously and positively. This kind of situation will not be solved by simply glossing over them. I suggest that clause 3 of the Solicitor general's Bill C-84 should be completely removed and that we should come back to the old Criminal Code wich provided for capital punishment in all cases of murder or attempted murder and during piracy acts.
Mr. Speaker, I believe this is a protection and a positive step we must take. This afternoon, I was listening to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) who said that capital punishment was something abominable and totally regressive, that it is regressive to speak about capital punishment, that we are being as violent as criminals. The minister has controlled information since the very beginning of this debate by referring chiefly to Professor Fattah's studies. He published a number of booklets that were sent to hon. members. Did the people who had the opportunity, the experts who were in favour of capital punishment get the same financial resources from the Department of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) to express themselves? No, only those who shared the Solicitor General's view.
Let us use his literature. In the booklet entitled "The fear of punishment", issued by the Law Reform Commission of Canada, it is said in page 73, and I would emphasize that this is a plea that the Solicitor General is using all the time in an attempt to convince members of the House of the value of and need for abolishing capital punishment, in the same kind of argument as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. The argument put forward by Professor Fattah, which the Solicitor General repeated many times like a real parrot, is that first, capital punishment is not an effective deterrent; second, it does not solve the problem and third, we should improve our deterrent methods.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring forward the following argument by beginning with a quotation. On page 72 of the booklet entitled "Fear of punishment" one can read, and I quote:
July 5, 1976

According to Ball (1955), "there is ample evidence that the complete cessation of police operations is quickly followed by a surge of crime and a chaotic social situation".
Andenaes (1965) . . .
Other examples follow. In Denmark, among other places, in Copenhagen, things have happened. I shall spare the House these quotations. I shall relate an incident that occured in Montreal on October 7, 1969, which is related in the booklet ordered by the Solicitor General, and I quote:
On October 7, 1969, the Montreal police went on strike; nearly 1600 officers and 600 policemen out of a complement of 3833 stopped working. The strikers were claiming wage parity with their Toronto colleagues. The work stoppage lasted 16 hours. During that time, there were nine bank robberies by armed people and seventeen qualified robberies in commercial establishments. A number of stores on St. Catherine Street were pillaged, in centre town. Crimes against property were four times higher than usual in this area. In others, the increase varied between 20 and 300 per cent. On the other hand, they went down in certain areas where people had reinforced surveillance of their stores and houses, certain establishments having moreover closed earlier than usual.
And more figures are used to show that as soon as there is a relaxation in police activity, there is an increase in the number and the seriousnous of crimes. This proves, Mr. Speaker, that the police constitutes a certain deterrent. Everyone recognizes this without a doubt. This is generally preventive force. I refer to the incident in Montreal where a ganster held a group of students hostage in a school bus. At that time, the Montreal Urban Community police intervened. There were called in. They tried to discuss with the criminal, but to no avail. The police forces were armed, the bandit was armed. Mr. Speaker, this was therefore an act of piracy where on the one hand a criminal committed an act of piracy by taking over a public transport vehicle, and this in a manner that was well organized, well thought-out, what we call premeditated.
On the other hand, there are the police forces, those that we pay with our taxes. These police forces are armed, prepared, trained, paid to protect private property, public property, and especially the lives of our fellow citizens. What choice is left to the policeman called in to the scene of this act of piracy by bandits in Montreal, where the criminal had taken over a bus full of children, and I repeat that they were school children? Shoot to kill? Not shoot and hope that the bandit will come to his senses, or else take roundabout ways to try to solve the conflict?
Mr. Speaker, if the bill is passed with clause 3 in its present form, the minister would like us to abolish the death penalty in the case of the bandit who is guilty of an act of piracy, who hijacks a school bus or a plane or a train, who threatens to run it off the tracks or to blow it up, who kidnaps Canadian school children. He is asking us to trust that the criminal will save the lives of those children. That is the first point. Here is the second point: he asks us to trust the police forces to try and solve that very serious problem of threat by armed criminals, but once again without risk, and therefore, I conclude that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) would ask, in a case of piracy, would ask the police force to simply watch the crime without interfering, without using their weapons, to just stand there to show that we have a police force.
I say to the Solicitor General, in conclusion, that it would be ridiculous for the police to put their lives in danger to catch somebody who threatens the lives of thirty
Capital Punishment
children, when they know very well that because of this bill and clause 3 even if they risk their lives and the lives of the children during the shooting, the criminal himself is in no danger. He is protected by the Solicitor General, in clause 3. He says that it is an old-fashioned crime that has not happened since 1900. Apparently he has not been in his constituency of Notre-Dame-de-Grace for a long time, Mr. Speaker. I say that to carry out its duty the police force needs the legal, if not the moral support of the government.
In the accompanying documents, the minister refers to several cases where police action must be reinforced, and there is proof how ridiculous the minister's argumentation can be. What appears even more shocking to me is that in the case referred to in Montreal, among others, we will all remember the press reports and the general outcry raised among the very ones who want the most probity, the most broadness of mind possible with respect to criminals. So there was a great many people, including journalists, observers, the League for Human Rights, the Solicitor General and such other people to blame police agents for having taken action too fast and, thus, having threatened the existence or life of anyone of the children who were in the bus. This, Mr. Speaker, is the height of absurdity! There are even people to blame police forces for having taken action not fast enough, or too fast, thus risking the bandit's life.
Mr. Speaker, that beats all! I understand the point of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Center. As far as he is concerned, we should be very understanding, we should be more trusting. He told us this afternoon that we had not reached the point where we should mistrust our neighbours and look under the bed before going to sleep at night. I understand him, Mr. Speaker, but I would like him to explain the logic in his argument. He claims the death penalty must be abolished in all cases. Oh, come on!
In this case, that, of the school bus, we are dealing with an act of piracy. Or of attempted murder, if not murder, because the police have to put a stop to it. Will the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre carry his argument to its logical end and disarm the police? I ask the question in all seriousness. Why let the police keep their arms when they run the risk of wounding children in the cross-fire when they try to capture the criminal? Why not simply stand there to prove that the criminal is doing wrong?
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre will tell me that it is a deliberate act and that, in any case, the criminal would have committed it. So, let us twiddle our thumbs and let him do whatever he pleases. Mr. Speaker, I would like the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre to see one of his children in such a bus. I would like him to tell me and to explain to me why policemen are armed in such a situation?
Mr. Speaker, this is my point. On the one hand, in the publicity it makes, the government tells us that we must strengthen the police measures and, on the other hand, he speaks about a deterrent. It says that an act of piracy makes no sense and, consequently, that its perpetrator must simply be liable of life imprisonment. Consequently, if there is a murder or a murder attempt, the death penalty will be abolished. Mr. Speaker, I claim that it is not an old crime, it is not something out of fashion, but it is an act that is committed almost every week now throughout the

July 5, 1976
Business of the House
world. The perpetrator of a such act committed in Canada should be recognized as being liable to the death penalty, as was provided for in the old Criminal Code. I urge my colleagues on both sides of the House to study this question very carefully.
As a conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I was saying at the outset, must a single act be committed, must dozens of people die or be killed following an act of piracy for the minister to recognize that it is a modern crime, a crime which could be committed tomorrow morning.
To finish my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like hon. members to understand that my amendment proposes that we simply revert to the application of the old Criminal Code. If, as the Solicitor General told the committee, it is true it is a crime which does not exist, which has not been committed in Canada since 1900, so why does he change the Criminal Code? It does not bother him, he might as well leave it as it is and the problem will be solved.
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) said earlier, we are accused of demagogy or, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre said, we are accused of getting angry because we present amendments or arguments.
But as far as I know, Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of every hon. member in this House to analyze each line of this bill since it is life and death issue, not only for criminals but also for innocents. Mr. Speaker, I think it is time for hon. members who analyze this bill only on the basis of criminals to analyze it on the basis of the protection of society and of punitive legislation, to the extent that people are punished according to the intensity or the gravity of the crime they committed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret that I seem to be late but I understood I was No. 2 on the list tonight. Now that I have the priority position I want to raise the question that I brought up in the House last Wednesday with respect to the proliferation of commemorative stamps being issued by the Post Office Department. There has been a growing concern and restlessness in the philatelic community because, as is well known in those circles, it is quite easy to kill the goose that lays the golden egg in the desire-

subtopic: POST OFFICE-APPLICATION TO OLYMPIC STAMPS OF PROVISION TO WITHDRAW TWELVE MONTHS AFTER ISSUE
speechtext: Is that not treason?

subtopic: POST OFFICE-APPLICATION TO OLYMPIC STAMPS OF PROVISION TO WITHDRAW TWELVE MONTHS AFTER ISSUE
speechtext:
Not in this respect, I might tell the hon. member. In the desire to make as much profit as possible there is a tendency to kill the goose that lays the golden egg. Whether the department is trying to reduce the soaring deficit in the Post Office Department, which I think is currently about $675 million, or to make a dent in the soaring Olympic debt which is close to $1 billion, I do not know. Certainly the practice is not enhancing Canada's reputation in the international philatelic community.
In the question on Wednesday I dealt specifically with the issue of the Olympic statue stamp which came on the market on March 14, 1975, and according to a quite specific arrangement should have been withdrawn 12 months later. In his reply the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) indicated that this interpretation was accurate-that there was an understanding with the association to which
Adjournment Debate
Canadian stamp collectors belong that new issues would be withdrawn following a 12-month period. When I drew attention to the fact that this $1 and $2 Olympic statue stamp was still available over post office counters, he revised the answer by saying it does not apply to Olympic stamps; indeed, they will not be withdrawn until one year following completion of the Olympic events.
As I have indicated, rather than enhancing the coffers of the Olympics, an over issue and over exposure of stamps means that the total return will be reduced. The market cannot possibly absorb the number of stamps being issued.
This matter came to a head in 1973. Dealers were called into a special meeting at the headquarters of the Post Office on December 5, 1973. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Bill Eyre, who is the manager of the philatelic retail products and market development section. The deputy postmaster general made an appearance to reinforce the significance of the meeting. Out of the meeting came a communique which purported to cover the matters that were raised. As set out on page 3, paragraph (e) of the memorandum the meeting reached the conclusion that the new public sales policy of the Canada Post Office to be explained in detail at a meeting on February 1, 1974, would mark the implementation of some significant changes. All stamps would be sold in a package format and would be available for 12 months only from the date of issue. That was the reply the Postmaster General gave to me last Wednesday before he issued the revised version. I have confirmed by discussion since last Wednesday with people who are knowledgeable in the field across the country that this is a restatement of policy upon which there has been no consultation.
The Canadian Stamp Dealers Association assure me that their understanding of the results of that meeting in 1973 are precisely the same as the conclusion I read indicated, namely, that there is a definite agreement with the trade that all stamps will be removed after 12 months exposure on the open market. It even goes further than that. The promise was made that any remaining stocks will be destroyed. Usually popular issues of stamps are sold out within a few months. Because of the over-issue tendency, the market has been adulterated.
I think whoever replies for the Postmaster General tonight, and I presume it will be the parliamentary secretary, will agree that it would be a much more profitable venture if the number of issues were kept on a marketable basis and if the promise that was made to the trade were kept, as has been requested.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always welcome questions and the chance to debate with the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) because he is very knowledgeable about the Post Office.
There may be some confusion here. Perhaps we can clear it up this evening. Postage stamps are divided into two categories. There are the philatelic quality commemorative stamps sold to all collectors, and the regular stamps used to prepay postage.
Philatelic quality commemorative stamps are sold from philatelic outlets and the headquarters mail order service for a period of one year, in the various forms such as full

July 5, 1976

panes, corner blocks, and so forth. In addition semi-annual pre-packs containing a single stamp of each issue are made up and sold for a period of 12 months. These also are sold only from philatelic outlets and the mail order service.
Regular quality commemorative stamps are usually sold out at post offices within a few weeks. However, a special situation has arisen with the Olympic $1 and $2 commemorative postage stamps (sculptures) which were printed in sufficient quantities to be on sale in post offices for a longer period in order to give full publicity to the holding of the Olympics in Canada. These stamps were on sale in post offices after the first anniversary of the date of issue. While they are no longer being supplied by our distribution depots, some post offices may be selling the residue until the supply is exhausted.
If philatelic quality stamps were being sold from philatelic outlets, other than the special packages, after March 14, this was in error. We are inquiring into this now, and if we find an error has been made it will be corrected immediately. I would appreciate any information the hon. member can give us to support an investigation of this kind.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST-ALLEGATION MR. BISSONNETTE IS LINKED WITH COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES OF CHAIRMAN OF ANTI-DUMPING TRIBUNAL

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST-ALLEGATION MR. BISSONNETTE IS LINKED WITH COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES OF CHAIRMAN OF ANTI-DUMPING TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refer to the question I asked on June 21 with regard to the activities of Mr. A. L. Bissonnette, a member of the AntiDumping Tribunal. My question arose as a result of inquiries made in this House by my colleagues, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. McKay) and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), relating to the activities of the chairman of the tribunal, Mr. Gauthier.
I realize that the next day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) made a statement with respect to the activities of the chairman of the Anti-Dumping Tribunal and with respect to Mr. Bissonnette, a member of that tribunal. Unfortunately I was not able to be present at the time of the statement and the questioning of the minister and it occurred to me there were some questions with respect to this whole situation which the minister might not have answered at that time.
We shall have to draw attention to the whole question of conflict of interest with respect to the order in council activity of the government, with respect to the activities, in this case, of the chairman and members of the board which might infringe the guidelines covering conflict of interest in relation to public servants. The minister was at great pains to explain that the conflict of interest guidelines did not apply to this particular area of quasi-judicial appointments.
What bothered me about the answers the minister gave at that time was that under the act members of the board are required to devote their full time and attention to the activities of the anti-dumping tribunal. In such a situation I find it difficult to come to terms with the minister's explanations with regard to the members of the board holding directorships in various corporations, as this

reflects upon their responsibilities to the appointments they hold. In the case of Mr. Bissonnette, the minister stated he had been asked to divest himself of his seat on various boards of directors, but it seems to me the government ought to give serious consideration to establishing a particular administrative procedure to deal with situations of this kind.
In cases of this sort, where appointments are made by order in council, particularly when there is a statutory requirement that those appointed should devote their whole time and attention to their duties, such persons might be required to make a declaration periodically that they had in fact refrained from carrying on activities other than those they were required to carry out under the legislation, in this instance as members of the anti-dumping tribunal. When the act is as specific as it is in this instance, it seems to me it raises an issue quite apart from that of conflict of interest.
We could discuss ad infinitum the question of the propriety of members appointed to any tribunal involved in export and import activities acting as directors of other corporations engaged, perhaps, in similar activities. We may question that, but it seems to me that in this particular case the point was missed by the minister that there was an explicit and specific prohibition against any of these members acting in any other capacity.
The point of my grievance with respect to the answer of the minister when he undertook, in response to my question, to give a full and detailed explanation of the requirements that the government felt were incumbent upon Mr. Bissonnette, is that there is only a request by the minister that he divest himself, subsequent to the disclosure of his activities, of his directorships of corporations. There is no coming to terms with government policy regarding whether or not there should be some administrative procedure by the government respecting order in council appointments, that such people in fact make a declaration, not necessarily of their holdings but whether they are contravening the statutory provision that they shall devote their full time and attention to their particular responsibility.
This question is very important to us since we find ourselves questioning people who have been appointed by order in council using government facilities and expertise for private purposes and interests. Notwithstanding the question of conflict of interest, it seems to me that this matter-I see you are rising in your place, Mr. Speaker-is one in which this whole question of devoting full time and attention to a position should be answered by the government.

The second point I should like to devote some attention to is that we should have an annual review of the investments or directorships that the various members of the board may have. It would be of some interest to the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar to spend some time reading the comments made in the other place on the subject of

conflict of interest. Possibly there are some areas that are not clear, but I think the two officers the hon. member mentioned did comply with the conflict of interest guidelines. They have taken notice of them, know what they are, and have answered all the clauses contained in the conflict of interest guidelines. This may not be satisfactory, and in the way he has raised the question there may be another procedure, but this has not been determined. It can certainly be considered when this is reviewed.
